subtopic: MR. MANDZIUK    OBSERVANCE OF 1964 AS SHEVCHENKO YEAR
MR. MANDZIUK    OBSERVANCE OF 1964 AS SHEVCHENKO YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I beg leave of the house to draw to the attention of hon. members an event in history important to all Canadians regardless of their ancestry, but in particular to those of Ukrainian racial origin. The Ukrainian branch of the Canadian family tree has designated 1964 as Shevchenko year to celebrate the 150th anniversary of the birth of Ukraine's poet laureate and national hero, who was born on March 9, 1814.
Some hon. members will recall that three years ago, on March 10, this house honoured my compatriots by granting me leave to address it briefly on the solemn occasion of the centenary of Shevchenko's death and to commemorate the unveiling of a statue in his honour on the grounds of the Manitoba legislature on July 8, 1961. The unveiling ceremony was performed by the then prime minister of Canada, the present leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), in the presence of some 40,000 people. Hence this is the year of celebration of his birth in Canada, the United States and in the whole free world. Last June the former president of the United States, General Dwight D. Eisenhower, unveiled a magnificent statue of Shevchenko in Washington, D.C. in the presence of some 100,000 people. Our own C.B.C. showed a part of this ceremony, and it thrilled the hearts of my compatriots.
On Wednesday of this week in Winnipeg His Worship Mayor Juba is issuing a proclamation declaring the 5th, 6th and 7th of this month as Shevchenko days in Winnipeg, and during these three days thousands of Canadians of Ukrainian and other origins will converge on the capital of Manitoba for three days of deliberations under the guidance of the Ukrainian-Canadian committee. On Sunday September 6 these people will again march to the foot of his statue to pay homage to him and to dedicate themselves to the
ideals of freedom they enjoy in this land, freedom for which Shevchenko prayed and fought but which was denied him and his people in their native land.
Shevchenko was a writer and poet who proved to the world that the pen is mightier than the sword. His prophetic exhortations gave birth to and have kept alive the vision of national unity and of his people's aspirations for independence. He was a patriot of the Ukraine but he was not a narrow minded nationalist. His fiery words, for which he suffered banishment to Siberia, condemned the imperialist policy and oppression of all Slavs by Moscow.
This branch of the Canadian family are again marching to the foot of Shevchenko's monument to proclaim to all their fellow Canadians that they bring to this nation their heritage, their ideals which have guided their race through a thousand years of turbulent history, ideals and visions which Shevchenko crystallized in his poetry and whose works became their national bible. We want our fellow Canadians to share him with them, to share his visions, to share him with all who are oppressed.
Our fellow Canadians may wonder why such universal adoration is given to this man here in Canada and in the free world by those who were forced to flee from their native land but who found a ready welcome and freedom elsewhere. Their complete loyalty is to the new motherland, but they are concerned about the land of their fathers. Shevchenko gives the answer in a poem written in prison before his banishment to Siberia. May I give you the English translation:
It makes no difference to me,
If I shall live or not in Ukraine Or whether any one shall think Of me 'mid foreign snow and rain,

It makes great difference to me That evil folk and wicked men Attack our Ukraine, once so free,
And rob and plunder it at will.
That makes great difference to me.
I thank you, sir, and this honourable house for giving me an opportunity of saying these few words on such an important occasion.

Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday, August 26, the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg on a question of privilege raised a matter regarding a report in the news magazine Time, as it related to a quotation from myself, and at that time said I was either talking through my hat or I had been misquoted by this magazine article, and that I should completely dissociate myself from it because, he said, that statement was a complete falsehood. Checking on the article to which the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg referred-and by the way I have the highest personal regard for him-I find that the article quotes these words:
"Mr. Diefenbaker refused to consult with his own party or to consider any reasonable compromise himself. His proposal for unanimity would give him the power of veto, and the lack of any time limit merely prolongs the agony. He disregards completely the normal democratic process of majority rule."

Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not always agree with the reporting of this magazine. In fact many times I find myself in disagreement with it, but on this occasion I find that they have quoted me, so far as I remember, exactly as I made this statement in reply to a question from a reporter for this magazine. I was not talking through my hat, nor can I dissociate myself from this statement because, as I understand it, it is a statement of fact.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is necessary to go back briefly, to review the situation by way of explanation, to August 4, the date I believe the party leaders first met in the Prime Minister's office.

I was going to state that the one criticism of this newspaper article in question is that it gives the implication that the leader of the official opposition never consults with his members. I had no intention of giving that interpretation to what I said. I was speaking to a specific point that had been raised by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg.
Mr. Speaker, the situation behind this question is that on August 4 the Prime Minister called a meeting of the party leaders to consider a proposal that had been made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, regarding a way to solve the difficulties for the immediate moment, and also give some definite formula for concluding the flag debate later on when the house would resume after a recess which he had suggested.
Without breaking any confidence that we have in respect of this meeting, I believe it is general knowledge that we could not come to any agreement. As a result I made an alternative proposal. This alternative proposal was not original with me, as I read it in a leading editorial in the Montreal Gazette that morning. It seemed a very reasonable suggestion by which all members of this house could honourably get out of the position they found themselves in, and which was becoming increasingly difficult with each continuing day of the debate.
Very briefly this suggestion was that the three maple leaves should be replaced with a single maple leaf, and the amendment to the motion bringing this to pass would be made by a member of the opposition; that the union jack be replaced by the red ensign to represent Canada's membership in and our belonging to the commonwealth, and that the Prime Minister should take steps to immediately declare all votes as free votes in the house.
We discussed this suggestion at some length, and at that meeting it was agreed that each of us would take this suggestion back to his party members. I did not regard this in any way as a matter of confidence, because one could hardly talk it over at one's own caucus on that basis so I did what we had agreed to do. I took the suggestion back to our party caucus and we discussed it. I went even further than that. I notified my own constituents that such a proposal was before us,

and recorded in the Red Deer Advocate, the newspaper of my home town, on August 8 a brief summary of what I have just said. I did this with the idea of getting a response back in order that I should have some sense of what my constituents would think about this particular suggestion.
I was dismayed some days later, I believe on August 12, when the hon. member for St. Mary stood up in this house on the orders of the day and asked the Prime Minister the following question, as reported on page 6719 of Hansard:
Would the Prime Minister agree to a meeting of the leaders of the five political parties represented in the House of Commons to discuss the Canadian flag?
That meeting would be called to reach a unanimous decision on the choice of a distinctive Canadian flag, other than the three maple leaves, which would then be submitted to the house by the Speaker, in order to dissociate that matter from any political partisanship-
-and that, within a set period.
In reply to this question the Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, we have already had useful meetings with the party leaders, and I hope this procedure can be continued.
Then the right hon. leader of the official opposition rose and said:
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. There was no question raised at this one meeting or at any meeting regarding the nature, kind and design of a flag. I am sure the Prime Minister, in answering as he did, did not intend to leave that impression.
Mr. Speaker, I was not only confused but upset by this statement, because to me it was in direct opposition to what we all knew had taken place at the first meeting, and on which we had acted, I think in good faith, in bringing this to the attention of each of our members. I was also disturbed by the fact that many members of the Conservative party were coming to me and others of our party, asking if there had been any discussion regarding an alternative design.

subtopic: ADJOURNMENT FROM FRIDAY TO TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 8
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is true that the meetings of the house leaders do not always produce conclusive results. We had a meeting this morning, part of which will have to be adjourned to a later date, but I am pleased to report that we agreed on at least one thing which is of importance both to the members of the house and their families, and the staff of the house. All the leaders, in the names of their respective parties, have agreed to the suggestion of the government that this house should not sit on Labour day. I therefore ask for an order of the house: That when this house adjourns on Friday September 4, 1964, it shall stand adjourned until 2 p.m. the following Tuesday, and that the relative standing and provisional orders be suspended in relation thereto.

The house resumed, from Thursday, August 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government he authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. More.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this marathon debate in the sure and certain knowledge that many of the points I wish to make have already been made, and that some of my brilliant ideas may have already been committed to the permanent record; but I think my ideas on this subject should be placed on record. I shall be using half an hour of parliament's time, whatever that
Canadian Flag
represents in money, and as repetition has always been rather abhorrent to me I hope I shall not say again many of the things that have already been said. Yet I am not completely out of sympathy with the prolongation of this debate until some semblance of sanity takes command of the situation.
For those who are not completely satisfied or not satisfied at all with the proposed flag, what other alternative is there but to continue to raise objections to the form in which this flag is proposed and to indicate that one more member at least has very strong views in this regard? I recognize, Mr. Speaker, that there is a certain amount of impatience in the country, in the press and even among members of the house with the extension of this debate beyond what seems to be a reasonable time, and on an issue that has nothing to do with our economic or social problems. I share this impatience, but the alternative of total surrender appeals to me even less.
The Prime Minister, who achieved public notice originally for his diplomatic ability, seems to have found one issue which he cannot or will not negotiate. I can understand his fears with regard to giving in a little and then a little more and finally becoming overwhelmed with objections to his plan. I see the position of the Prime Minister at the moment as somewhat like that of the driver of a team of runaway horses, hanging onto the reins with both hands and afraid to let go one hand so he can pull on the brake which would save him. This is a simile which is familiar in many stagecoach westerns, but it strikes me that it represents the present situation exactly. The brake in this case is a better procedure for establishing a distinctive Canadian flag than by a simple majority vote in the House of Commons on a single flag design. I hope the brake will be found before the whole stagecoach overturns.
All of us, I believe, are affected by our racial and historical backgrounds in our approach to the question of a flag. My ancesters came to this country from northern Ireland 115 years ago. They brought with them at that time a strong loyalty to the crown and to the empire, as it then was. That loyalty has continued to be strong in the subsequent generations, and is strong in the riding which I represent. It is not unanimous in my riding but it is a strong feeling, and I find myself in the rather fortunate position, which some other hon. members do not seem to enjoy, of being able to speak for my riding in one voice as my constituents would have me speak. I am thinking particularly of other

Canadian Flag
hon. members who feel they should speak as they think the decision should be made regardless of whether it is in agreement with the feelings of their own people or their own personal beliefs.
In spite of the backgrounds that all of us have brought to Canada, I think I speak for everyone when I say there is only one ultimate loyalty, and can only be one ultimate loyalty, and that is to Canada. I am sure I speak for all my constituents and for a good many, if not all, Canadians when I say that.
Most of our people have come to accept the red ensign as the flag of Canada, not because it bears the union jack but because it is our flag. The difference may seem to be subtle but it is very real. I believe this is where a lot of the problem originates; not because it is a flag with the union jack, or whatever there might have been on the flag we learned to respect in school and later, but because it is our flag. That is one of the reasons it is difficult to get a change of opinion among many people as to what the new flag should be or whether we should have one.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that most of the people I represent would accept another flag, in spite of their personal preferences, if it had general acceptance and would unite our country in its goals. That is my own position. It must by now be apparent that the proposed new flag in the main resolution does not carry the general support either of the house or of the public. From what I have heard it carries the majority in the house, at least if the votes that have been indicated are correct, but that does not mean that it carries general acceptance. The majority is not enough in this country, and it never has been.
The rights of the minorities were strongly protected at the time of confederation. They were protected to the point where it was one of the basic tenets of Canadian confederation that the majority should never be able to overrule the minority on any of the questions which concerned the person, the individual. This is the basis of confederation; therefore in this particular issue the question of a flag which affects each one in a personal way cannot be settled by a simple majority vote.
The best evidence of the fact that the flag does not command a great and overwhelming enthusiasm in Canada is the effort of the Minister without Portfolio to drum up support for it. It has been very obvious in the last few days, from the questions and the answers received to them, that there is not the acceptance in Canada of the flag the government would like to see, particularly if the minister has to go out and sell it after it has been

flown in so many places. I have seen it on car aerials; everyone has seen it. Surely it does not have to be sold. If it has to be sold then I cannot see that it has any general acceptance.
It is my own personal view that Canada should have a new, distinctive flag, and that before 1967. Furthermore, I am confident that a design can be found which will be generally acceptable. I have seen several proposals and I really believe some of these have the strength, the design, the purpose, and the historic symbols which would be acceptable. I only mention in passing the type of proposal made by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska. Perhaps it is not completely acceptable as it stands, yet it represents something that could join us together. There are others also. I have seen several designs, and I am not picking one or the other. However, I do believe that such a design exists, a design which would satisfy those who want to retain the elements of the British background, and those who want a new flag. I think it can be found, and I am going to propose how it should be done.
To speak for a moment of the Canadian red ensign, I have taken a consistent view throughout this debate and in my public statements that unless and until some other acceptable design is found, the red ensign must remain and continue as the flag of Canada. We have to do this. We cannot exchange, as has already been stated by several hon. members, one group of dissatisfied Canadians with another. There is no future in that.
I have one other belief which I want to state. Some may believe it heresy, but I do not believe that our boys in the services fought and died for a flag. I believe they fought and died for their country, and I stood beside enough of them to know. However, I know they did fight under the red ensign, and there is no reason to haul it down unless it can be replaced by something which will give us what they died for, and that is a greater and better country.
I would like to make a few comments about what I believe to be the real and fundamental cause of our differences and difficulties in connection with the flag. I want to ask first whether all this fuss over a flag is over the flag alone, or does it represent something deeper? I believe the hard core of the difficulties in this matter is exactly the same as it was at confederation 100 years ago, and 100 years before that. It is exemplified in the views of those people who see the development of Canada as a struggle for the

ascendancy of one racial group over the other; and in spite of 100 years of partnership there has been precious little willingness or ability to bridge our differences. The proof of this belief is that the presence or absence of the union jack in a new flag is the real point of difference. Unless there is some unanimity of thought and some great desire to build a better nation, I do not think we can get together on this problem.
It has been said earlier in this debate that Canadian unity is an objective of this new flag. I ask, where are we to find this unity? Certainly it is not in forcing the choice of a majority upon an unwilling minority by a parliamentary vote. Neither is it in asking the people to make a decision on one or two designs chosen by political parties. Neither is it to be found by forcing the view of the majority on a minority by means of a plebiscite on stated questions or on stated flags. I believe we should first find out whether Canadians generally want a new flag. If so, then parliament will have to set up a committee to make an irrevocable decision. I believe such a committee should be an extraordinary one set up to deal with an extraordinary situation. It should be broadly based, and it should represent the many conflicting views held across this country. A time limit would have to be set upon the deliberations of such a committee-
Would the hon. member permit a question? Does he not realize that this was done 20 years ago, when a committee sat for two years on this question of a national flag?

Yes, I realize that; and I realize that after it had sat, the Liberal government of that day decided to take no action on the recommendation. I think that answers the question. The committee voted 23 to 1 in favour of a certain flag but the government would not accept it. The wrong approach was taken; there was no prior agreement to accept the decision of that committee. I would ask the hon. member, if he has not already made his contribution to the debate, to make it after I have sat down.
On a question of privilege I must advise the hon. member that I had occasion to make a speech on this issue, but I do not wish to take part in the filibuster.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
How many years ago?
Twenty years ago?

In this debate.
Canadian Flag

The hon. member has used the word "filibuster". That expression was used on several occasions by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he made his speech recently. I took the trouble to look up "filibuster" in the dictionary to find out what it really meant. I was considering using the same word myself; because if we are conducting a filibuster I think we should admit it. But we are not. This is not a filibuster. I intend to read to the hon. member the definition of "filibuster" and perhaps he will understand that he is using the word incorrectly. As described in Webster's third edition it means "the use of extreme dilatory tactics by individuals or groups in an attempt to delay action by a majority in an assembly".
Hear, hear.
Precisely.

I disagree entirely with the hon. member about that. I say there have not been extreme dilatory tactics used. Some members opposite do not want to have a debate on the flag. They wish us to simply vote on it. But I think this is one of the most important issues to have come before this parliament for many years.
Mr. Speaker-
Sit down.
I do not intend to get into a debate with the hon. member. He will have a chance to make his contribution when I sit down.
It might be helpful to the hon. member if he were to listen to me. It might shorten his speech.
I did not hear that last comment, but I assume I did not miss very much.
Nor did anybody else.
Why refuse to hear it?

I shall continue by saying this. I know some of my colleagues in this chamber are anxious to have a new flag. They will say that a committee would merely cause delay and result in no action being taken. They are looking back, as is the hon. member for Nickel Belt, to a previous Liberal administration 20 years ago.
On a question of privilege.
There is no question of privilege.

I think the truth should be known. The committee which sat 20 years ago was not a Liberal committee.

Canadian Flag
I should like to know what kind of a government it was, then. Other words have been used to describe it, but I thought it was headed by a Liberal prime minister.
To be completely truthful about this, the committee referred to by the hon. member was not a Liberal committee; it was a house committee composed of members of all parties.
As a member of that committee I must inform the house that it had a Liberal majority.

I thank the hon. member for Kootenay West. Not only did the committee have a Liberal majority, but so did the house. I only wish to say to those who think nothing would happen, that it would be much better if two years from now we were to have a unified country than it would be to have a divided country with a new flag. I think that is the essence of the problem now. Furthermore, if the fear of delay is so great, is that not an admission that there is something to be lost and that there are arguments against the adoption of a new flag?
I wish to conclude my remarks by outlining my views on the vote which will take place when the debate on the subamendment is completed. In order to do this I will have to express my views on the main motion and the amendment, not in detail but in summary. As I stated, I do not believe the proposed new flag has the general support of the people of Canada, and I shall be obliged to oppose the main motion. I can support the amendment because it is broad enough to include my proposition that we should determine the single question whether or not a new flag is wanted by the people of Canada.
The subamendment contains four proposed questions, none of which include the question I should like to see proposed, that is, the alternative that another flag may be considered and another design substituted. The four questions which are there relate only to the proposed flag and to the retention of the red ensign. However, the wording of the subamendment reads "that among the questions to be placed before the people" shall be the four which are detailed. I think this does not exclude the suggestion I have made, and I shall be able to support it. I should, of course, like if possible to support the subamendment moved by my hon. friend from Regina City.
In conclusion may I say we are engaged in a debate. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate at the end of the question period

repeated words which the Prime Minister had used earlier. He said he wanted every member of the house to have an opportunity to express his views on this subject. If this is the case, Mr. Speaker, how on earth can it be called a filibuster? I do not believe I am engaging in a filibuster; but if it is a filibuster, and if it will produce some change in the obstinate stand the Prime Minister has taken on his three maple leaf flag, then I am privileged to have been a part of it.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in support of the subamendment before the house I do so as an elected representative whose responsibility is, I feel, to convey to this parliament the consensus within the riding and on behalf of the people within that riding. It is my intention to vote in favour of the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City and seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk, the subamendment being that the amendment be amended by adding thereto the words:
And that in any such plebiscite, among the questions to be placed before the people should be the following:
1.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?
2.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritage of both founding races?
3.	Are you in favour of the three maple leaves design?
4.	Are you in favour of a one maple leaf design?
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this motion I will endeavour on behalf of my constituents to convey not only their feeling of support for the Canadian red enstign, but I will also strive to assure them of their rightful opportunity to declare their choice, whatever it may be, concerning a national flag.
In addressing myself to this motion I would refer to a statement reported in the Canadian edition of Time of March 15, 1963, which states that the Prime Minister at a press conference for foreign language editors in Toronto, when replying to the question "What would happen if the Liberals failed to achieve a majority", had this to say; "In that very unlikely event, all good men will have to come to the aid of the country". I repeat that statement made by the leader of a minority government, that in the unlikely event of that result all good men would have to come to the aid of the country, and I say that statement was never more applicable than it is today.
If the Prime Minister was sincere in his concern for all good men and women; if he was sincere in his desire to maintain unity and shape the destiny of our great nation for

generations to come, then I say the Prime Minister should heed his own words and let the people come to the aid of the country and voice their opinion concerning a national flag. Never before in the history of Canada has such an issue affected so many people. Never before has an issue become so emotional, and never have so many people expressed their opinions pro and con, or actively taken a stand or engaged in a campaign to support the issue, which is the choice of a new, distinctive Canadian flag.
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that the flag which flies over the Canadian people, whatever that flag may be, should be a flag chosen by the people, a flag that the people respect, a flag that the people consider represents our democratic freedoms and our way of life; a distinctive flag, representative of the history and heritage which we cherish; not a flag chosen by a political leader, a flag purported, rightly or wrongly, to be the personal choice of one man, a flag which is now considered to be merely a political pennant; not a design accepted, mistakenly, as a tangible form of appeasement to a group who desire only, and with justification, to attain recognition of their culture and heritage and who strive to attain national unity which will afford them the respect and recognition they so justly deserve as one of the two founding races in early Canada. Mr. Speaker, I quote an excerpt from the Amherst Daily News of Friday, December 29, 1961:
Q. You say the Liberals are working on a design.
Mr. Pearson replied:
Oh, there are hundreds of designs. But it would be the responsibility of government to make up its mind which design it would submit to parliament.
Q. How would you poll the people on this?
To this question the Prime Minister replied:
We would poll the people when we have a general election. And if they don't like the idea of a distinctive Canadian flag which can't be mistaken for that of any other country, they'll let us know in no uncertain terms.
If the government would agree to this method I am sure the Prime Ministers words would be very well justified. The people are desirous of making known their feelings in no uncertain terms. At the outset of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I stated that it was my intention to assure the constituents in my riding that they will have their rightful opportunity to declare their choice concerning a national flag. This opportunity can only be afforded through a national plebiscite. To vote in support of the motion I feel is the
Canadian Flag
only democratic procedure this parliament can follow to determine the right action which will legislate for time to come a flag emblazoned by accepted symbols, a Canadian flag of the people and chosen by the people.
In urging that this issue be placed before the people for their decision I wish to present certain communications from the riding I represent, that will substantiate the stand I have taken in support of this motion. The first communication states:
I wish to register my plea with you to uphold the red ensign as Canada's flag.
Please do all in your power to give everyone a chance to voice their wishes by voting on this issue.
I would repeat that request, Mr. Speaker:
Please do all in your power to give everyone a chance to voice their wishes by voting on this issue.
The following letter is from the Cape Croker Indian reserve:
As a member of the Cape Croker L.O.B.A. 1132, in your riding, I wish to state my stand in defence of our Canadian ensign.
Our flag, the ensign, is a truly distinctive Canadian flag. The red background challenges any country in the world to try to better our freedom, equality and democracy. The union Jack in the honour position honours all treaties, alliances and pacts up to the present day, and the Canadian coat of arms flying freely in the field signifies the freedom and equality of all people in this great country.
We do have a democracy. We do have the right to vote. No one man or one man's parliament can decide Canada's future or fate. The fact that Mr. Pearson does not choose to accept this Canadian way of life is certainly sufficient reason for knowing that his choice of a flag would not be fit for democratic, freedom loving Canadians.
I reiterate what has been said before. We do have a democracy. We do have the right to vote. No one man or one man's parliament can decide Canada's future or fate. A veteran who wrote this letter to me had this to say:
As a Canadian citizen and a resident of Bruce county, I feel it my duty to write to you and express my feelings, and my family's feelings, regarding all the ''bunk" and "ballyhoo" about a Canadian flag. We already have a Canadian flag, a copy of which I enclose.
It is recognized as well as any flag as the "Canadian flag". When our convoy arrived in Scotland in November, 1941 the first thing I noticed in the harbour was a green maple leaf on the funnel of a ship and our Canadian flag, the red ensign, at the mast. Long may she fly.
Are we to deny this veteran the right to vote in support of his choice of a national flag, a right for which he fought, served and sacrificed during the last war? Many Canadians will never be persuaded or convinced

Canadian Flag
to accept a flag other than the flag which now flies proudly over our land. For many, such as the mother who wrote this next letter, there must be the opportunity to confirm their opinion at the polls:
I feel very strongly that the Canadian red ensign represents so much common sacrifice that we cannot sit idly by and see some other flag forced on us by any minority group. Therefore we trust that you, our elected representative, will use your good influence to bring this matter to the attention of those concerned. One of my sons sacrificed his life under this flag of ours and I feel I want no other.
No personal political pennant would ever be accepted by this proud mother.
By conducting a plebiscite we will give to those Canadians other than the descendants of the two founding races the opportunity to exercise the freedoms and rights which are theirs; the freedom to make their own decision and the right to endorse the same, either as native born Canadians or as new Canadians who have attained citizenship in the land of their choice.
One group of Canadians, Mr. Speaker, which must be heard and considered by the administration of this country is the Indians. I represent two Indian reserves in my riding, and they feel that the flag proposed by the Prime Minister completely ignores the flag under which their treaties and pacts were signed. Vernon Jones, a former chief of the Cape Croker band, thinks all Canadians should have an opportunity to accept or reject it. This Indian constituent has been most adamant in expressing his feelings. He says:
We are looking forward to retaining our flag the red ensign. We are natives of this country and have great respect for the flag which we went through two world wars under, so I say hands off the red ensign. We are known as the red men or red race, so I feel we are represented on the ensign. So I am writing you hoping that French flag will never fly because we are not represented anywhere on it. We have not yet surrendered and that is all the white flag means to me.
So we are asking you to ask Mr. Pearson to forget about his flag, because we don't see how he can fly it without some bloodshed. Some of us are willing to fight and die for our flag and Mr. Pearson wouldn't want discontent in this country.
Another letter which I have received from an Indian reserve sets out in some detail the concern of the Indian for the retention of the red ensign and the union jack. This letter says:
Dear Sir:
It is with great concern that I view what I call the Pearson flag. Looking back in history, the Indians of Canada have, with good reason, fought for the union jack and the red ensign.

In the war of 1812 we fought for the British. The world war of 1914-18. The last world war of 1939-45. In the above mentioned wars many of our people did not come back. The transition of the independence of Canada was not felt by our white neighbour as it was by the Indian. As an example, while the supreme tribunal was the privy council of England, we felt secure that an independent tribunal was or had the guardianship of our treaties.
Since the Supreme Court of Canada became the final court, the Indian has lost the right given him under the Jay treaty, agreed upon by the British crown, the United States and the Indians of North America (treaty No. 166).
When this treaty was presented to the Supreme Court of Canada, it was nullified, on the grounds that the war of 1812 nullified all treaties between the U.S.A. and Canada.
Although that war did not directly concern the Indians they are the ones who paid the penalty.
All or most of our treaties end with: these provisions are to hold good, as long as grass grows, the water flows and as long as the British government is in existence. If the union jack is deleted from the Canadian ensign it may be disastrous to the rights guaranteed the Indian by that flag.
The people will not accept a flag without voicing their opinions either by a vote or through the representations of their member of parliament. Yet we had been told at one time by the Prime Minister that we must accept his flag or he would take this issue to the country. Why, if the government are not afraid to face an election over this issue, do they endeavour to suppress the representations made by members on behalf of constituents who favour other than the three maple leaves design? If they are confident that this is the design favoured by a majority of Canadians, why then do they fear expressions of support for another flag by members from this side of the house and label them as filibustering? I have had letters from constituents stating that the writer will not respect in any way a flag considered to have been rammed down the throats of the people.
If we are a true democracy, then we must have the mandate of the people. If we have a parliamentary government, then we must place this issue before those who sent us here. If there is to be justice and tolerance, then all Canadians must be allowed equal opportunity to their opinions. And if there is freedom of the individual then we who sit in this house must ensure that freedom will be upheld.
Like my colleagues I have received many letters and petitions with regard to this issue. Are the Prime Minister and those who sit on the other side of the house going to ignore these expressions of public opinion, such as those voiced by the Royal Canadian Legion and the Legion women's auxiliary, organizations like the I.O.D.E., women's institutes and other church groups? Will the protests of the

Canadian corps, the Canadian patriotic association and ethnic groups go unheeded? What reply will be given to those who express personal opinions or actively support a flag other than the three leaves design?
I refer now to the many individuals who have seen fit to contact their member of parliament: the elderly in the nursing home, the war widow, the farmer, the new Canadian and ministers of the church. Many of these communications, such as the following, are brief and to the point:
Dear Sir:
I am not one of those ungrateful Canadians of British ancestry who would care to dump the red ensign, rather I would like to retain it as our national flag.
Communications such as I have read at this time have continued to come in as this debate has progressed, and they run to many pages. Of the many petitions, letters and resolutions among them, there is a common expression for the retention of the red ensign and a desire for the opportunity of expressing opinions at the polls. This resolution of the ladies auxiliary says:
We the members of the ladies auxiliary of the Canadian Legion would like to voice our opinion of our flag.
We would like the red ensign flown over Canada for our flag, always.
I have a copy of a letter which was addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) which reads:
The undersigned lodge of the ladies Orange benevolent association duly moved and resolved, we petition you Mr. Prime Minister, and the government of the dominion of Canada in respect to Canada's flag.
We do petition herewith, and desire it to be known it is our firm desire to keep the union jack as the flag of Canada. If a distinctive flag must be adopted, let the Canadian ensign, which has already become known around the world, be the one chosen.
The ladies Orange benevolent association continues to loyally support Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, Queen of Canada and the flag of our empire, our beloved union jack.
Requesting your due consideration to the above resolution.
Mr. Speaker, I have endeavoured to convey the feelings in the riding of Bruce. Speaking personally, I would repeat in this chamber what I said recently in a speech regarding the flag-for those who served under this flag I have respect and appreciation for their sacrifice in defence of our country. This is the flag under which I myself would be proud to serve, and as a father I would be proud to see my sons serve under the flag which is recognized as being symbolic of the Dominion of Canada since 1867.
Canadian Flag
Mr. Speaker, I stand firm in my support of the Canadian red ensign. However, if the Canadian people see fit to choose another flag I will recognize and respect that flag as a patriotic Canadian. I ask, though, that this choice of a flag be given to the people of Canada.
In closing I say to the Prime Minister, all good men will have to come to the aid of the country.
Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have participated in any of the debates relative to the proposed adoption of a new flag for Canada. I should like to say to my colleague from Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) that I think he was far too modest in his opening remarks when he somewhat deprecated the kind of contribution he was going to make. I found his points, as usual, extremely well taken, carefully thought out and helpful, and the kind that a good parliamentarian should make from time to time.
I had the same reaction to the speech of my colleague the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Loney), which was also thoughtful, positive and helpful.
Mr. Speaker, it is an unfortunate thing that we have a development in Canada, much of which is the responsibility of a press which probably writes its material a little too quickly, and is over conscientious and concerned about deadlines, which has led them to believe that any item discussed for any length of time by the people's representatives is in some way an indication of obstruction or delay. One gets the same reaction from the press comments about the speech from the throne; it is said that it drones on and that all members go over the same sort of things. Such writers are forgetting that before our assembly was an assembly of responsible government, it was a representative assembly in existence to represent the people of the country. When we have these things developing which stir and stimulate public opinion it would be strange indeed if the public's representatives passed their days in silence. I think it is extremely useful to have the kind of contributions which have been made to this debate. I am proud of the fact it is colleagues of mine who have carried the major burden of this debate, and who have led the public in the discussion of this very important question. I am proud of them.
In the main, the contributions that have been made have been helpful and have sought to minimize an unfortunate action and

Canadian Flag
an unwise decision of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the government, which has clearly endangered the unity of the country. We have always had this problem in Canada. Always we have had to have wise and good leadership which could prevent the cleavages from becoming so deep that they could not be healed.
It is appropriate that this House of Commons be directed along the lines which the two hon. gentlemen have suggested, and on this day, when we come prepared to turn our thoughts to the anniversary of the great Charlottetown conference which took place 100 years ago tomorrow, and which the Prime Minister is very properly attending as the representative of this house and his government.
Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time unity has been threatened. The situation was not easy 100 years ago. Many times since we have had problems that have created grave danger. I think it is incumbent upon us to make sure that no utterances of ours will do anything to pit one Canadian or group of Canadians against another so as to weaken the always frail fabric of confederation which binds this great but heterogeneous country together.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) was kind enough to express concern about the party to which I belong, and to give us advice. I am not one of those who are considered excessively partisan. Sometimes I am told that I am not sufficiently partisan; but as he was advising us I was thinking of an even greater danger. I would hope that his party would not contribute to the kind of thing that the great Sir John Thompson spoke about as the greatest threat which could befall the political life of a country such as ours. Sir John Thompson, one of the three great Nova Scotians who became prime minister of Canada, said something that strikes me as being extremely apropos at this very moment. He said:
"The one calamity above all others which stands before this country is that political divisions should follow the division of race or the division of religion. The one danger which menaces the future of this country and the union of this country, now so happily being accomplished, is that men should stand arrayed against each other on the question of government, because they differ with regard to religion, because they differ with regard to race.
Mr. Speaker, I refer to this situation as one which we must all avoid.
I thought too that a colleague of mine, the hon. lady from Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Wadds), not long ago picked up the very same

theme that one of our great statesmen of the 1890's enunciated, when she said:
Let us clarify what we mean by unity-not rigidity, not force physical, or legislative, but understanding, a concentration on our common purpose, not on petty irritations, hurts and pride.
We speak of national unity as if it were a building we have to construct quickly, preferably cheaply, and certainly without aching muscles and red-rimmed eyes. A building which once constructed will shelter us from all modem harm.
Unity is only partly physical, mostly mental and emotional, ever changing, ever demanding, but so worth while.
We today, Mr. Speaker, are striving for a measure of unity. We are trying to reach a solution that will not irritate, that will not cut deeper the wounds that might have been made. That is a big part of the effort which is being made by the opposition party, the oldest party which Canada has and the party which was founded and based on a great understanding, a co-operative working arrangement between the leaders of the two founding races of this country. This is what we are seeking. This is the kind of suggestion that we have in the subamendment in our efforts to come to a decision on this matter, and if we have to discuss the matter at great length let it be discussed at great length, because it is a very important matter.
The higher value of a parliamentary institution is not speed and efficiency. The higher values by far are democracy, compromise, consensus and the proper serving of the people we represent. I believe that the party of Macdonald and Cartier, the party which took the lead in confederation 100 years ago tomorrow, was wise in its suggestion that once the error was made by the Prime Minister the whole matter should be put to a plebiscite. I believe that a plebiscite has become a good and useful thing, an important contribution to salvaging all that we can from a situation that was created by the government and especially, I am sorry to say, by the Prime Minister, a man for whose career and personality I have always had the highest regard. It is unfortunate that he, who in a long and fruitful career was so successful in reconciling differences, so adept, so skilled, so devoted in finding solutions among opposing suggestions, should be the very man in this year 1964 who has interposed one of the great divisive factors in Canadian politics. It is all the more regrettable because it was all so unnecessary, so unfortunate in its timing and so damaging in its method.
The house is naturally having difficulty in following the lead of the government in this matter. I am one of those who in happier,

calmer times would have sought to suggest to his people that perhaps our country could well do with a distinctive flag. I am one of those who would be prepared to say that the symbols which are dear to me could be retained by me and my people without necessarily being retained on a flag. We would all do much by way of compromise. But faced with the situation that was presented to the house and the country, even those who belong to that school had no other choice but to oppose, and I can do nothing more than oppose with voice and vote resolutions A and B.
There is something more to a plebiscite than a mere effort to find a consensus which the house is not able to produce, although that is surely a part of it. The house is clearly divided, deeply divided on this measure which has been brought before us. There is something more to a plebiscite than the fact that the people of the country should have the most thorough and complete participation in the adoption of a symbol-and the flag is a symbol. That is a big part of it. But there is something else. It is an unfortunate thing that we have seen political partisanship develop about the design, and throughout the country we hear the expression "Pearson's pennant". It is an expression I have never used, nor do I intend to use it. I do not think we improve our public life by such remarks any more than we did much for Canada by the expression "Diefendollar", something which I think is now very hard to obtain for reasons which we shall not discuss in this debate.
But the selection of a symbol for the country is not the kind of thing which a minority government does, and when it is succeeded by another government, either majority or minority, then has its choice set to one side. It would be ridiculous to have various prime ministers and various parties with their flags. We do not want a Liberal flag or a Conservative flag or a Pearson flag or a Douglas flag. We want a Canadian flag. So I think that on this important matter we should do that which other countries do in a constitutional way-entrench a decision once taken by a parliament. And to bring the decision of parliament to the people for their vote will give to it the greatest permanency, because we know that no parliament can bind its successor and a mere resolution on the order paper followed by a vote would not give that permanency which a plebiscite would.
Canadian Flag
I am one of those who believe that in this instance advocacy of a plebiscite is extremely apropos and is essential to a proper solution of the problem which is before us, because we want a flag upon which there is not only a consensus but with regard to which there is a realization that it is going to be ours for a long, long time. I agree with the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Loney) that we should honour any flag which is adopted. I avoid expressing my artistic reaction to the flag envisaged in the resolution before us because it contains symbols that could conceivably be used in a flag which would be adopted. I am convinced in my heart of hearts or, to use an old expression, I have a feeling in my bones that the flag set out in the resolution will never fly officially in this country. I believe this is in the cards. But I am not convinced that in the decent processes of democracy, along the avenues of compromise and down the paths of good will and understanding, some sort of new flag may not emerge. If it is adopted properly, honourably, democratically and fairly I am prepared to honour it and to encourage my children to do so. To find a method we have suggested the plebiscite, and I commend my colleague from Regina City for the suggestions which he has put forward. The four choices have been read. There are those who believe a plebiscite should contain more, but I would be a little happier if there were fewer choices.
The question, "Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?" is a very appropriate selection for the first question. I have never understood those who maintain that the Canadian red ensign is not a distinctively Canadian flag. I have had some few opportunities to be abroad, to attend the United Nations and other places, serving this country in some small way. Never have I seen the slightest hesitation that the Canadian ensign was in fact the symbolic representation of our country. Therefore I believe that whatever happens-and I am going to talk about the suggestion of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken)-the Canadian red ensign cannot and should not pass from use in this country until the people of this country have had a right to express themselves thereon.
It is unfortunate that sometimes we have allowed ourselves to get into that frame of mind whereby we have no flag at all. Of course we have had a flag, and it has had legal status. It has had recognition, and it is ill advised to suggest otherwise. If it is unsatisfactory, that is a different matter. Let us

Canadian Flag
find avenues to explore that question; but we get nowhere by presuming that the Canadian red ensign is not in fact and in law the flag of this country. I personally find it a rich and colourful flag. I thought the beauty of this parliament hill on Dominion day, with 66 flags flying, was most impressive.
The Canadian red ensign is rich and appealing. It has history, but perhaps to some it has things which bring a negative response. Perhaps some people find there things which point to a period in their ancestors' history which was disturbing. If I thought only of the days of Culloden I would not think too much of the union jack either, because never was there more butchery than was practised by the arrogant Sassenachs of the south against my ancestors of the north. But I do not see that in the ensign. I see in the ensign an evolution of one of the greatest political communities the world has ever seen.
I see there this country which led the world in the evolution of dominion status. I recall too, and it was only proper that it should be, that French speaking subjects of the crown many years ago were given civil and political liberty that English speaking subjects of the crown in England itself were not given. I see there the struggles of Robert Borden against some pretty thick-headed people in the colonial office. I see through the years the evolution of the commonwealth, where Borden pressed the case for equality among the members of the commonwealth, and where one of Borden's successors, our own Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), in another stage, successfully pressed the case for equality of peoples within the commonwealth.
These are things we can see, and perhaps we Canadians have failed in not becoming a little bit more emotional about the symbols of our existence. I heard the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) say the other day that the young people of this country, the vast majority of the younger generation, sought a distinctive Canadian flag. That may well be. Possibly we have failed, especially those of us who were educators, to point out to them the distinctiveness of the flag we have. Certainly our American cousins are not remiss in expressive nationalism, if we might call it that, and we may have failed in this through neglect.
It should be to the young that the national symbol means the most. Like the hon. and gallant member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) who spoke the other day, we express our personal preferences; we then move on to pledge ourselves to support
[Mr. Maequarrie.l
a solution which is arrived at by ourselves and our colleagues in the proper way.
I would suggest that when we arrive at a distinctive flag, either through the means suggested by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) or through a simpler or more elaborate plebiscite, we will be able to pour upon that symbol the emotional affection which many Canadians feel for the Canadian red ensign and for other symbols which have been used in this country.
I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Calgary North, the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) and others, and referred to a little while ago by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, of referring the matter to a committee for serious, careful study is an excellent one, a committee which would function while the House of Commons, its parent, would deal with other matters of equal but different urgency. I would hope that that committee would be able to make preparation so that it would overcome some of the mistakes which were made by the Prime Minister and the government in his and their exercise in flag unfolding.
I would think if this committee would call to its aid as counsel-if I may use the American expression-two heraldists, two historians and two artists we would avoid the terrible shock which many artistic people felt when they saw the symbol before the house in the main resolution. If this were done it would be a useful step. I would hope that, after careful deliberation and thoughtful consideration, such committee would come out with a pretty widely accepted design, and the next step would be for that design and the Canadian red ensign to be submitted to the Canadian people in the next general election.
If that were done the Prime Minister would have fulfilled his commitment in having brought forward the matter of a distinctive flag. The House of Commons would have fulfilled its duty by bringing order out of confusion, unity out of division and agreement out of bitterness, and then the people of Canada who are the ones who must have the final voice would be able to express their opinions. This I think would be something of which Canadians could be proud. This would be a fine preparation for 1967. It was recognized that a mistake had been made. It is a mark of greatness to recognize errors and I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has

made a profound one. I believe there is a widespread feeling in this country-I was about to say "in his party", but I would not presume to go as far as that; I do not know- to this effect. But, I would be greatly surprised if this deep feeling had not permeated his party as well.
I can see a committee of this house doing useful work. I would hope it would be selected with the best of intentions; that it would have a vice chairman from the Conservative party. I would think that a distinguished gentleman such as the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) might be given the second place on such a committee and I am sure the government could nominate some distinguished member from its own side, such as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Stewart) or the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Pennell) who could give leadership to such a group in considering some of the ideas put forward. We have witnessed, I think, a real expression of serious concern among the Canadian people that this matter should be dealt with, that it should be dealt with properly, and that there should be no surrender to political expediency and no excursion into partisan, racial or religious bitterness. We want no part of any of this. No member can be accused of failing in his duty if he stands up and makes clear his opposition to some of the efforts which have been made in this chamber with regard to the flag proposal. I think the House of Commons can come out of this with its reputation enhanced as the great forum for the expression of Canadian opinion. Is there division here? Is there disagreement? Of course there is, because this is what we find among the Canadian people.
The best thing would have been for the Prime Minister never to have made his move. Better he had done other things. Better he should have moved to bring us into the organization of American states. I would have followed him in that, by voice and vote regardless of what any of my colleagues chose to do. Better he had found some way of reforming the Senate, as was promised in 1893. That is a long standing promise. But this action having been taken, there is still room for a little reaction, a little reconsideration, much give and take. I can see at the moment no better arena for this than the microcosm of the house itself, which is a house committee. Such a committee, untrammelled by rigid time limits-I believe
Canadian Flag
there would be a sufficient sense of seriousness among its members that it would not be necessary to lay down an arbitrary time limit-would, in my opinion, be well qualified to find a solution to this problem. I think there is a feeling among our people that a solution should be found but that it should not be a partisan solution, a mere rushing to a vote in the House of Commons. I cannot help recall a saying by Sir Robert Borden 50 years ago that some who were most anxious for votes in the house were least anxious for them in the country.
The Prime Minister is not here-he is in Charlottetown where, to tell the truth, I should like to be myself. But I do appeal to him to retrace his steps as far as necessary, because otherwise he will leave a record which will mar a great contribution to Canada. He is a diplomat. He is a man who, I still believe, is a great Canadian. The little series of bunglings among various cabinet ministers is unfortunate and regrettable. And seemingly it is eternal. But what is more important is something which strikes at the very vitals of the country, namely national unity. And if the Prime Minister could come out of this with his genius for compromise, retrace his steps and accede to the pleas of those who are sincere in their submissions, then out of this unfortunate division may come another example of Canada's ability to work together when the chips are down, party with party, race with race and creed with creed. If so, the flag debate was well taken up and, if so, we shall have proven ourselves. I think, Mr. Speaker, we can do it.

Before I proceed with my remarks in this historic flag debate I should be remiss if I did not draw the attention of the hon. members of this assembly to the very fine, scholarly, academic and thought-provoking speech we have just heard from the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie).
Hear, hear.
It is regrettable that a man with his vision and foresight could not be in that great city of Charlottetown today with other members of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Duty comes first.

I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that in making this contribution to the debate I will be brief. I spoke on July 3 in this house. At that time we were engaged in a flag debate which was to terminate at the end of five days. I spoke on July 3, just two

Canadian Flag
days after Canada celebrated its 97th birthday. The subject of the flag was very much in the thoughts of all Canadians at that time. We had portrayed to us on the front lawns of this building a memorable display of 66 Canadian red ensigns. I said then that I would vote in favour of the Canadian red ensign but at the same time I realized there were many Canadians who had other views on this matter and that I would be in favour of a referendum to try to settle the problem. I also said on that occasion-and if I might be pardoned for quoting what I said:
It would be very simple and inexpensive to hold a plebiscite. It could be held at the time of the next federal election at little expense. You would simply walk in to vote, be given a ballot with the names of the candidates on it and you would be given another slip of paper with three or four flag designs in colour and you would simply mark an X opposite the one you preferred. I believe the method adopted in the province of Alberta, which is referred to as the transferable vote, could be adopted whereby you mark your choices first, second and third. There would be no problem in that regard. I know each Canadian would say, "I will be loyal to the flag which the majority of Canadians choose."
And later in my speech I said:
I suggest to the Prime Minister that if he is bound to bring in a new flag he should start over again with a clean sheet. He should set up a nonpartisan committee to represent Canada and introduce a new design for parliamentary approval, not a government design. If he does not want to do that, he should withdraw the resolution that is before the house now. This is the last day of debate, at the moment. He should allow the members to reassess the whole issue during a summer recess. Let us go home to our constituencies; let us think about this very serious matter. Let it simmer a bit and then come back and decide where we go from there.
As I read those words again, Mr. Speaker, I think how much better it might have been had we taken the recess and come back here to reassess this very important problem. What has happened since? Many hon. members have spoken in this house. We have heard many very thought-provoking speeches. I think of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather), the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Doucett); and, yes, even the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) and many others. These men spoke with sincerity, with beliefs, with ideas, with feeling in their hearts, and gave suggestions to this honourable chamber as to what they thought ought to be done with regard to selecting a distinctive flag for this country. This is the seventeenth day of the flag debate. I hear it said-it is said to me quite often-"Why is this flag debate going

on so long?" I would remind hon. members and the people of this country that the United States recently debated the American civil rights bill for 72 days. I am sure our debate is every bit as important to Canada as that debate was to the citizens of the United States. We should endeavour to maintain unity, bring our peoples closer together and give to all a greater feeling of national identity and purpose. These, Mr. Speaker, are the things we have to try to bring about in this debate.
Much has been said about the cost to the taxpayer of continuing parliament while this debate is in progress. May I remind you, sir, that most of the costs of this house are on a yearly basis, so whether the house sits or does not sit adds little to the cost of its operation. I would agree that those who are employed on a sessional basis represent an added cost. This may involve secretaries. However, Mr. Speaker, over the past few years parliament has been sitting so continuously that they have been on a yearly basis anyway. Therefore, it is a minor cost to the country for such sessional help as the page boys and the cleaning staff. There may be a small extra cost in connection with paper for Hansard, and printing; but apart from that I can see no additional cost to the operation of this house in discussing such an important subject as we now have before us.
Members are here because they are sincere in their purpose; they are here to debate this great cause and this important subject that is before us. So, Mr. Speaker, the debate has continued. We have heard briefly from some hon. members of the other parties. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) favours a new flag. In his case it is the Pearson tri-leaf if necessary but not necessarily the Pearson tri-leaf; he would prefer a single leaf because this, he says, would symbolize unity. For the Social Crediters, the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) says flatly that a minority government has no mandate to impose any flag upon the people of Canada, and he demands a referendum. Then there are the members of the all-Quebec group, the Creditistes. The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) has pledged support to the Pearson design. Again there is contradiction and dissatisfaction, because he says, "We are not satisfied with the proposed design; we would prefer another. Anyway, the flag will not strengthen unity".
Then even the Prime Minister himself has doubts on this matter. I wish to refer to just one of the many contradictions in his

speech, when he said, "When the house has come to a decision members will abide by it and do all they can to obtain its universal acceptance". In other words, "Accept or face an election; and having accepted, help sell it to the country". What a flag-conceived in secrecy, sired in coercion and born to be sold. On the subject of being born to be sold, we heard all about this the other day when the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) was questioned about the sale of thousands of tri-maple leaf bumper stickers. He took it upon himself to circulate from his own government office, with his own government help, an advertisement asking his supporters to buy these maple leaf bumper stickers by the thousands. So it was certainly born to be sold. To realize this we only need look at the great promotion that has been brought about in the sale of this flag from newsstands and other places of business; how they have been flown on the aerials of cars, and so on. There has been a great promotion in order to put this tri-maple leaf design before the people of Canada.
We have had a subamendment put before the house by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More). This subamendment was simply introduced in his good thinking to bring to the attention of the house how a plebiscite could be held. Among other things, what would be on this plebiscite or this ballot which the people would receive when they went to vote? I do not like to take up the time of the house, but the four points included in this subamendment were:
1.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?
2.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritage of both founding races?
3.	Are you in favour of the three maple leaves design?
4.	Are you in favour of a one maple leaf design?
These suggestions, amongst other things,
were included in the subamendment he put before the house. Public opinion in regard to this matter has crystallized in the last few weeks, Mr. Speaker. I would humbly suggest that there is no argument whatsoever as to whether Canada should have a distinctive national flag. I believe this is practically universally accepted. We should certainly have it for our centennial, which is just a few years away-our 100th birthday in 1967. Indeed, we should have had it many years ago, and it is regrettable that the Right Hon. Mackenzie King in 1945 when he, by order in council, said that the Canadian red ensign would be the official flag of Canada, did not stop there; but he went
Canadian Flag
on to say "to be flown from government buildings either within or without Canada". If he had left out of his statement that last little clause this matter would have fortunately been settled in 1945.
I think we have failed badly in our educational and training fields. We have not taught the children in our schools about Canada's flag, how to draw it, and the history behind it. This has been forgotten and overlooked, possibly because it was never officially declared to be Canada's flag. This minority government and its appointed Prime Minister saw fit to introduce the flag resolution that is now before this parliament, and rightly or wrongly they must bear the full responsibility, because the parties on this side of the chamber did not bring it in.
The government of the day saw fit to bring this resolution before the house and I should like to quote what the Prime Minister had to say in this introductory remarks on June 15, as reported on page 4318 of Hansard. He said this:
The government's responsibility is to decide on policy, to present that policy to parliament for consideration, and they hope support, and to stand and fall on the decisions parliament takes. If parliament decides that it cannot support a government on a matter of major policy, our system does then provide for a referendum, a referendum to the people in an election.
So that point was made quite clear in the introduction of this flag resolution.
I commend the Prime Minister for his aspirations and desires in this regard. We have only to note one paragraph a little later on, when he said:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that a national flag of the kind described in this resolution, that will be exclusively Canadian, will bring us closer together: give us a greater feeling of a national identity and unity. Today especially, as Mr. Massey has reminded us, we need faith and confidence in ourselves as Canadians, with pride in Canada, devotion to our country. I believe that the adoption of this resolution will help to produce that result. If I did not deeply and sincerely so believe, I would not be introducing it into this House of Commons.
However, more and more each day his aspirations, goals and desires are not achieved. If his goal in this case is that of national unity and if that is what he wanted, it is abundantly clear without a shadow of doubt that some other method to achieve this aim must be sought.
The problem seems to arise from two sources, as I see it. As I said before, there is no doubt but that people do want a distinctive Canadian flag. However the problem which confronts this parliament is, first of all, how this resolution was introduced, and

Canadian Flag
second the particular choice of the proposed flag.
With regard to how the resolution was introduced, I think that if a poll were taken it would bring out the fact that practically everybody disagrees with the method of introduction of this resolution. Let hon. members opposite ask some of their sincere and loyal supporters, or the members of their own party, whether they agree with the method of introduction of this resolution. The hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) had this to say on August 24, as reported at page 7180 of Hansard:
I would point out that we never saw any details of this flag until Votes and Proceedings of May 26 were issued on May 27. The opposition saw this design as soon as we did. If this denotes that the Liberal party caucus has given its approval to the design in question, I would like to know when it did so. I attended all the caucus meetings and the design was not shown and, as I say, we did not see it until Votes and Proceedings appeared on May 27.
I cannot understand why or how a party would expect to have unanimity and support for the introduction of a flag resolution even before its own members were consulted. The same hon. member also said that at many of their meetings the Liberal party never discussed the question of a new flag. It was never an election issue in many parts of Canada. In my own riding the flag was never an issue in the election campaign, and I am sure there are many hon. members here who were never asked to declare themselves on the flag issue; nor was it an issue in their election platforms. There is plenty of evidence to show that this resolution does not have the support of the members of the party which introduced it.
This brings me back to the same point, that it was not so much the problem of the flag as its method of introduction, this take it or leave it attitude: This is for Canada, this is what we are giving you and this is what we want you to accept. It seems to be a known fact that the Prime Minister has received thousands of letters pointing out that he has gone about this in the wrong way. I think there is no doubt but that this is the way this great problem has arisen, namely the method by which the resolution was introduced, and second, the choice of the flag itself. I sincerely believe that if a more attractive flag had been chosen, one with a more artistic design or with more history and tradition behind it, it would have been more acceptable. At the same time I realize there is a difference of opinion over the choice which was made. There may be many who

like it, but there are many more who do not like it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, how is parliament to deal with this problem? What must be done? A very important matter has to be decided. I say it is up to the Prime Minister, who is the leader of the government, to make the move and to decide what he feels is best in this regard. I was very happy to hear the Prime Minister say that a free vote would be taken among his members. This is a reversal of his previous stand, but I commend him for it. On May 19 last the Prime Minister made it clearly understood that the life of this government depended on the outcome of the flag question. He said, as reported at page 3337 of Hansard:
I have pointed out, and I think I should make it quite clear, that when the government submits to parliament a matter of policy-and this is certainly a matter of policy-the government must stand or fall on the result of the decision of the house.
However, three months later he came before this house with an entirely different position and said that any vote on the flag question would not be considered by the government as being against party discipline and there would be no question of an election, whatever the result of the votes. So the whips are off; the way is clear. It is a free vote.
On July 3 I challenged many of my good friends on the Liberal side of the house to rise in their places and express their views on this very important matter. I challenged the hon. members for Durham (Mr. Honey), Brantford (Mr. Brown), Renfrew South (Mr. Greene), Carleton (Mr. Francis), Wentworth (Mr. Morison), Halton (Mr. Harley) and Hastings South (Mr. Temple) to rise in their places and give their views. I now challenge them again to get up in the house and make a speech on the flag, because as I say the whips are off and the way is clear. I know that, sure as I am standing here, the constituents in their ridings want to hear from them.
I suggest it is not enough that you be a spectator; your constituents want you to declare yourselves and take a stand. I know what my constituents would think of me if I did not make some observations during this debate. Being aware of the fact that the vote is to be a free vote they would ask what is stopping me from expressing my views and why I do not declare myself. They would say: Now that you are being allowed to vote freely, we want to hear from you and know your stand on this matter.

Mr. Speaker, we have only heard from 27 members out of 128 in the Liberal party. There are 101 members on the government side of this house who have not declared their stand on this flag issue.
Mr. Speaker, may I interject? That is perhaps slightly untrue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
