speechtext: Order. May I direct the attention of the hon. member for Norfolk to the fact that the hon. member for Wellington South has the floor, and he should first seek permission of that hon. member before interrupting to ask a question.
I will give him that permission, Mr. Speaker.

Thank you. The hon. member stated that the constituents of the members on this side of the house do not know anything about the stand we take. It so happens, and I speak for myself, that I have written my constituents personally, and that letter has appeared on the front page of all the newspapers in my area. The people know exactly how I stand and why I take that stand. I direct the hon. member's attention to that fact. Thank you ever so much.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that interjection on the part of my hon. friend from the town of Simcoe. He and I are graduates from the same alma mater, and I have great respect for him and appreciate what he said. However I should like to ask him why he has left it to the press to make his stand known rather than voice his opinion here in the House of Commons where it will be recorded in Hansard so that everyone will know exactly his position?
Mr. Speaker, we have heard from only 27 Liberal members. There are 101 Liberal members from whom we have yet to hear. We have heard from only one cabinet minister, plus the Prime Minister of course, in his introduction. In respect of a major historical debate on an issue of such importance to the people of Canada why do we not hear from members on the front benches, and from more members supporting them on the government side? I do not understand why there is such a delay in their expression of opinion, now that the vote has been declared a free vote.
I feel it is my duty, as a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, to recommend any procedure which, if followed, may aid us in solving the impasse which confronts this parliament. The people of this country are tired of hearing about the flag debate. They want the debate concluded, and
Canadian Flag
we should do everything we can to suggest ways of solving the difficulty. I might say that we have already done so. The leader of this party has moved an amendment to the main motion, proposing a plebiscite. I have heard the pros and cons in respect of such a plebiscite, but I must say that the only democratic way of deciding such an important issue as this is by a national referendum. Many views and ideas are held by the people of this country, and even families are split on this issue. The provinces are also divided on it. Therefore I feel the only democratic way of handling the problem is by allowing the people themselves to decide by plebiscite. The people could go into a quiet booth, mark their ballots and make their own choice.
Mr. Speaker, I realize there are arguments against holding a plebiscite. I have suggested that a plebiscite be held, and have heard people say that we are the elected representatives sent to Ottawa to take a stand and to make a decision. I think the answer to that argument is that this is a very important issue, involving a moral and personal choice, which 265 people out of 20 million could not decide. How are we going to have unity in this country if the decision is made in that way? This choice, once made, is not one that can be changed every two to five years, or as the government changes. Once this issue has been decided the resulting flag will remain as Canada's flag for all time. Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that we must allow the people of Canada to settle this important issue by means of a plebiscite.
Many people suggest that by holding a national referendum we will divide the country. I think this whole matter must be taken out of the political arena. I do not think a choice by plebiscite would be as divisive as a choice by 265 representatives here in the House of Commons. I think if a committee is formed to decide on the designs from which a distinctive flag is chosen by plebiscite, there will be very little division. I think the committee, as suggested by many members, would be of great potential value, and perhaps should be composed of seven members from the Liberal party, five members from the Conservative party, and one from each of the N.D.P., Social Credit and Creditiste parties, making a total of 15. I do not think it would be necessary, but perhaps a similar arrangement could be made in respect of senators, making the membership of the committee 30 instead of 15.

Canadian Flag
Mr. Speaker, I think the whole flag issue should be sent to that proposed committee for consideration and report to parliament within a reasonable time, perhaps three to six months. If that committee after its consideration could report unanimously back to this house, the debate could perhaps be limited to five days. If the report to the house was based on a committee majority of 80 or 85 per cent I think that report would receive the support of all parties. If that committee was unable to come to a unanimous decision, or a decision of an 80 or 85 per cent majority, this matter should then be referred to the people in the form of a plebiscite. The duty of the committee would then involve a decision in respect to the flag designs which would appear on the ballot for the plebiscite.
I would go one step further and suggest that once the plebiscite had been held and all ballots been cast the ballots should not be counted on a regional basis, but sent to Ottawa and counted on a national basis, so that no area or province in Canada could be associated with a choice in respect of a specific design. The decision would have been made on a national basis only.
As a member of the opposition, Mr. Speaker, I have done my best to make some recommendations and suggestions which I feel it is my responsibility to present to the house. We are at an impasse. We are at a point where parliament must make some decision. After talking to the people of my riding, other members of the house and friends, and having done a little soul searching on my own part, I think these are the best recommendations I can make to the leader of the government whose responsibility it is first and foremost to make a move so that the impasse will be broken.
I must make it clear to the Prime Minister and his supporters that, above all, members of the official opposition want a strong Canada made strong by each province, Quebec being one of them. As a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition it is my responsibility to try to suggest some way for the government to get out of the impasse. An explosive situation it is. The people of Canada want the flag debate ended and pressing legislation attended to. Therefore I beg the Prime Minister to accept the ideas, the compromises, the suggestions that have been made to him not only by myself but by many other hon. members. I appeal to him to take them to heart so that his record will not be marred for all time.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

I am asking this question purely for information. The hon. member suggests it would be possible to have a plebiscite with all the ballots being sent to one central point so that no one would know how any part of the country had voted. Would it not be necessary to identify the ballot boxes right back to the polls so that you could ensure the validity of each of the ballots, and carry out a check with regard to ballots issued, ballots used and so on? In other words, does the hon. member really think it is possible to send all the ballots to Ottawa as he suggested and still ensure the ballot count?

I think that is just a technical problem that can be overcome. I am sure it could be worked out, in the same way as all the ballots being sent to one central point in a province. They could all be sent to Ottawa. My thought is that we want to get away from the regional idea because we do not want to know what part of Canada voted for one flag and what part voted for another.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on the amendment to the amendment which deals specifically with the question of designs to be submitted to the Canadian people in a plebiscite. Before making any remarks in this connection I should like to refer to the fact that when I spoke on August 13 I was not allowed to finish the remarks I had planned to make, and since the subject matter is quite pertinent at the present time I should like to conclude what I had intended to say then. I wish to refer to a suggestion I was going to make on August 13 to the Prime Minister and which I assure you, Mr. Speaker, is intended to be helpful.
I want to say to the house, to the Prime Minister and to the government that I believe this matter can still be settled. In my opinion the procedure would be to appoint a committee which would be entrusted with the selection of designs for reference to parliament, with parliament then being asked to approve a flag on the basis of a two thirds majority vote. I do not know whether anyone remembers what I said at that time, but simply to remind the house may I say it was my suggestion that no decision of parliament on a question as important as a change in the flag, which is tantamount to changing the constitution and certainly of equal importance,

should be made on the basis of a bare majority but rather on the basis of at least a two thirds majority. I was about to say at that time that the matter could then be completely removed from the partisan political realm. From time to time the committee would bring designs to parliament until one was found which was acceptable to two thirds of the members. Those views which I had intended to express at that time are applicable to the situation which exists now.
It could be argued that this would be tantamount to a Conservative party veto, and I acknowledge that it is. But I do say to the house categorically that the Conservative party does not yield to anyone, certainly not to any other party, in its desire to do any and every necessary thing to contribute to the unity of this country. That is the question which I believe is before us at least to a certain degree-the unity of the country.
Many other developments have taken place in the period of a little over two weeks since I last spoke and I am going to refer to them later. Just before I resumed my seat two weeks ago I had been expressing disappointment over the fact that more ministers had not participated in this debate. I wondered why they had not spoken in defence of their position as members of a government that has submitted a resolution to the house which, from every point of view except urgency, is the most important resolution submitted to the house since I have had the honour to be a member.
Important, yes; urgent, no. It is important because it represents much to many Canadians. To some it represents their participation in two world wars. To some it represents their participation in the first world war and their recollection of that war. It brings to mind the betrayal of treaties. It brings to mind the rejection of the proposition that the pledged word of nations is of no account. It brings to mind the rejection of the principle enunciated by the German chancellor of that day that a treaty was merely a scrap of paper. I would remind the house that Britain and France fought hand in hand in that war, that France was invaded and Britain honoured her commitment and rushed to her defence.
To some people it represents memories of the second world war. It represents the recollection of a long period of training and then the events of D-day and subsequent events. To some citizens it represents the sacrifice of life itself by a member of their family. In the shire town of my native county a man and woman live today who lost two 20220-473
Canadian Flag
of their three boys in the battle of Britain, when Britain stood alone. They wish to keep alive the symbol of sacrifice contained in the union jack.
My mail continues to contain many messages urging reconsideration by the government of its apparent desire to discard and destroy our present distinctive flag, the red ensign. With all the conviction of which I am capable, I urge the government to reconsider. I am, however, not hopeful that they will. But letters are continuing to come to me and I believe they will go on. Many people found it difficult to believe that the union jack would be completely eliminated from the government submitted design.
As I said, this is the most important resolution to be brought before the house since I have been here. I do, however, deny the urgency of it. As a matter of fact in my opinion it is not urgent. It is something that should be carefully considered by everyone within the sound of my voice now and who may be in this chamber at any other time.
I repeat it is most astonishing, most disturbing and most astounding that ministers of the crown have not taken part to a greater extent than they have in this debate. This debate has been boycotted by ministers. It is a matter of the throwing away of symbols which have been used for many years; it is one of the most serious things, and I for one am not able to understand or comprehend it. Every minister should get up and explain this. It is our duty to demand that they do, and it is their duty to do it. This they have not done, and I state here and now they should have the courage to speak in this debate and make an attempt to justify their position.
One minister has spoken, one in 25. In my opinion he is one of the best known ministers, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp). He spoke relative to the subamendment and I have some comments to make regarding his remarks. The particular paragraph, among others, to which I refer and take exception, is in that portion of the minister's remarks found on page 6963 of Hansard for August 18. These are the words:
I invite my hon. friends opposite, and particularly the Leader of the Opposition, to abandon their negative role, which gets its best representation by this futile subamendment and which is doing so much damage to his party-

Hear, hear.

Canadian Flag

If you
get any consolation out of that you are welcome to it.
-and for that reason to the country, and join with the Prime Minister in achieving another great step forward in our development as a nation.
I have not neglected to quote the last phrase, since it obviously is his own biased and prejudiced opinion. I might have done so, but I do not care to quote the minister out of context. I now refer to his argument.
I take exception to his statement that the role of the opposition is negative, especially in this subamendment. That is not the case.
In support of this contention I quote the subamendment. It is positive, very positive. It is most definite. It makes concrete suggestions relative to the designs to be considered by the Canadian people in a plebiscite. It enumerates them, a, b, c and d, and it leaves room for more. For information and emphasis I quote the subamendment:
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the words:
"and that in such a plebiscite among the questions to be placed before the people should be the following:
1.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?
2.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritages of both founding races?
3.	Are you in favour of the three maple leaves design?
4.	Are you in favour of a one maple leaf design?
That is the subamendment referred to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as being negative. I ask this house and I ask you, sir, is that not positive? It includes the so-called Pearson flag as one design. It includes the red ensign. It includes a modified version of the ensign. It includes a one maple leaf design. What could be more positive? What could be more explicit? I draw the attention of the house to the use of the words, "among the questions to be placed before the people should be the following;" in other words the subamendment is not restricted to the four choices that are indicated. More may be added if in the opinion of the government there should be more. I would rather expect that there might be more designs which it would be considered advisable to submit to the Canadian people, and ask for an indication of their preference.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce also referred to the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition that a more distinct and more prominent fleur-de-lis might be contained in a modified version of the ensign, and I
[Mr. Flemming (Victoria-Carleton) .1
quote his words as found at page 6960 of Hansard:
To the people of Quebec this suggestion by the Leader of the Opposition-and I have heard it echoed by a number of speakers on the other side, none of them French Canadians-must have appeared as a clumsy and gratuitous piece of appeasement; it must have appeared to my French Canadian friends as a bone thrown out to a troublesome minority to keep them quiet.
I resent the suggestion of the minister that this constitutes appeasement. It does nothing of the sort. It constitutes a recognition of the facts of history, history that has been recorded not for 100 years, 200 years or 300 years, but for 400 years. That is the recognition that this accords. The minister said that this is a question of appeasement. The only thing I am going to give him credit for is making a speech and stating his view. He is far ahead of most of his colleagues in that respect, because that is more than any other minister of the government, excluding the Prime Minister, has done in this debate.
What is the cause of this silence, which might propertly be considered a filibuster of silence?
Oh, oh.

There
is one thing about this: They are listening to me a lot more attentively than they do to the hon. gentleman with his back to the wall over there. Is it because they cannot justify their position? Is it because they were not consulted? Is it because they are afraid of the next general election that they do not wish to have their views recorded on Hansard and then be obliged to face the people? Are they afraid to explain and justify their stand?
Those are the questions which they might properly answer, and if they disagree with these assertions let them get up and say so in this debate. Some of them are noted for their vocal ability, and some for very little else. Let us hear what they say and see how they look.
In a previous speech I referred to the fact that there was little if any record of any commitment by the government during the last election to bring in a distinctive flag. The hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), himself a Liberal, has confirmed my assertion. No Liberal has disputed him, no Liberal has answered him. Therefore I submit that what they should have done, if they wanted to bring in a design different from the one we have been using, was to go back and see what there was by way of examination and investigation of this particular thing.

I find that in the years 1945 and 1946 a committee studied the whole question of a flag. We have men in this chamber who were sitting here when the debate on setting up that committee took place. We have men in this chamber who were members of the committee itself. We have men who were members when the committee reported. I have indulged in some research on the subject, and I am going to give the house the facts which have come to light in my examination.
First of all I want to give the names of the committee members, and I quote from page 256 of Hansard for March 26, 1946. The hon. members of that committee were:
Messrs. Beaudoin, Blanchette, Castleden, Emmer-son, Gingues, Gladstone, Hackett, Hansell, Harris (Grey-Bruce), Herridge, LaCroix, Lafontaine, Mac-donnell (Muskoka-Ontario), MacNicol, Martin, Matthews (Brandon), McCulloch (Pictou), Mclvor, Reid Smith (Calgary West), Stanfield, Stirling, Thatcher' Warren, Zaplitny.
Those were the members of the committee. And I should like to point out respectfully to the house, because it is of some interest, that there are two members of the present parliament who were members of that committee- the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). This brings me right to the question I was discussing two weeks ago when objection from certain Liberal members in a certain quarter of this house caused the Acting Speaker to rule I did not have unanimous consent to continue. I find that the hon. gentleman was a member of the 1945 committee, an extremely good reason for asking the Secretary of State for External Affairs why he has not given us the benefit of the information he must have secured as a member of the flag committee in those years. Why has he not been impelled to contribute to this debate and tell us about the findings of that committee? Why has he not given this house some idea of the points raised by the various people who appeared before that committee?
I fail to comprehend his silence. Surely, he will speak up before this debate closes and tell the house the determining factors which led to the selection of a design for a national flag at that time. We shall await with interest the remarks of the hon. gentleman on this subject.
But we are fortunate in one respect. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) is a member of this parliament and he was a member of that committee in 1945-46. He has not been compelled to maintain silence, and he has not maintained silence. He has spoken in this debate, and hon. members will

find his remarks recorded at the beginning of page 4888 of Hansard for Tuesday, June 30, 1964. The part of the speech to which I refer will be found beginning in the second paragraph of the second column at page 4890, and I can do no better than refer to those remarks. He stated that no single party which has placed a proposal in its program for a distinctive flag for Canada had ever defined what it meant by a distinctive flag. So far as I am concerned, we are using a distinctive national flag at the present time. It is the Canadian red ensign. I acknowledge that everyone does not agree with this proposition. The hon. member for Kootenay West suggested that this had added to the confusion and to the division which exists even within parties with regard to this matter. He suggested that the situation emphasized the need for adoption of unusual procedures so that the final result may be satisfactory to the people of Canada. There is nothing wrong with that. He then mentioned that he was a member of the committee whose job it was to bring in a design, and he proceeded to discuss other matters which I think are of great interest. He told us that the committee heard many people, including representatives of the college of heralds, or persons informed about the procedure of the college of heralds. He told us that after all those who appeared had been heard, the committee considered 2,700 designs submitted by various people. There was a great deal of interest in the question. Now I will pass on to the house the recommendations of the committee of that day:
That this committee recommend that the national flag of Canada should be the Canadian red ensign with a maple leaf in autumn golden colours in a bordered background of white replacing the coat of arms in the fly, the whole design to be so proportioned that the size and position of the maple leaf in relation to the union jack in the canton will identify it as a symbol distinctive of Canada as a nation.
That was the recommendation of this committee after the examination of 2,700 designs. Here was a committee, composed as I have stated, which brought in its decision by a virtually unanimous vote. To make this clear,
I might tell hon. members that the committee reached this conclusion by a vote of 23 to 1. That, without question, constitutes virtual unanimity. At least, that is my considered opinion on the point. Among the members of that committee were representatives from all the provinces of Canada and from both founding races of this country. They were people whose background is similar to the backgrounds of many hon. members of this

Canadian Flag
house today. They constituted a cross-section of the membership of the house at that time and I believe they can be considered, as far as their various interests were concerned, to reflect a cross-section of the parliament of today. I cannot understand why the recommendations of that committee were not implemented. That would have solved this question for all time.
Well, I suppose it might be said that 19 years have made a difference and that the reason which justified the committee's conclusions then do not exist now. I do not agree.
I believe the reasons which brought about the conclusion in 1946 were present then and are present today. There is no reason why a flag based on the committee's recommendations should not be put forward as the flag of Canada. This is one of the recommendations of the subamendment.
I stress the need for permanency. It has been referred to by my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) this afternoon. We in this parliament surely do not want the recognition of a symbol which we think another government might discard. This selection would conform to the second choice mentioned in the subamendment. I would advance the idea that since this design was considered 18 years ago as being appropriate, surely it is appropriate now. Was it ever considered, I wonder? No one seems to know. It is a question we should like to have answered. Again I wonder why some ministers have not spoken. I wonder why the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) and the minister of northern affairs (Mr. Laing) who represent British Columbia, have not spoken. Will they get up in this house and say that British Columbia approves the so-called three leaf Pearson flag design?
Incidentally, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) was a member of this house in 1946 and I presume he had knowledge of the report of the committee at that time; I am unable to find any record of his disagreeing with the report. However, 18 years after, apparently he does not agree with it. I should like to have him explain to the house the reason for his change of mind and change of heart. There are other members here who were members of the house at that time, but they do not need to do any explaining. One is my hon. friend from Huron (Mr. Cardiff) who spoke, and spoke well, in this house a few days ago. He advocated the setting up of the committee 18 years ago and he was undoubtedly in favour of the report of the committee when presented. He still favours the adoption of the flag design which

that committee recommended. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) was a member of the committee then. He undoubtedly supported the acceptance of the committee's report which brought in the recommendation to which I have referred. He too has spoken in this debate, expressing the same opinion as he held 18 or 19 years ago. That is not all. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was a member of the house at that time.
He undoubtedly favoured the design recommended by the committee. But he did more than that: He moved a second amendment to the motion to set up the committee at the outset, in which he proposed that they be instructed to include the union jack in a prominent place in the design of the flag recommended to parliament. The Speaker of the day ruled that amendment out of order. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we know that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition has not changed his mind; he has no explanations to make.
A further examination of the record of the parliament of 1945-46 reveals the name of Mr. Benidickson, the man who I presume is my hon. friend the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. So apparently he has had a change of heart, because he is now against something which he supported 18 years ago. It would be interesting to have him get to his feet and explain the reasons for this. Then we have the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard). Presumably he favoured acceptance of the report also. As I said before, that included the design as given in the speech of the hon. member of Kootenay West, which I have just quoted. The hon. member for Ottawa East might properly explain his change of mind also. Last but not least we have the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has not participated in this debate. Rumour has it that he will be voting for the design of the Prime Minister, the government and the Liberal party. He voted for the setting up of the committee in 1945-46; he voted to accept the report of the committee. But now, according to rumour, he has changed his mind and is going to vote for the design submitted in the name of the Prime Minister. I wonder whether he would like to explain to the house why he has changed his mind, or does he wish to deny that he is going to vote for the Prime Minister's design, and declare that he will vote for the subamendment?
I do not wish to overlook many people, Mr. Speaker, so I should like to have the

Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) lake part in the debate. Since coming to this house I heard him at one time, when he was on this side of the chamber, declare unequivocally his preference for the flag which floats over the peace tower of this building. That was within the last four years. He has apparently changed his mind. It would be of interest to all hon. members if he were to give his reasons; and I am sure it would be of special interest to the premier of Newfoundland.
Hear, hear.

Last, but certainly not least, there is the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh). Where does she stand? I am one of those who expect much from her. Surely changing the flag of a country is important enough that she should contribute to the debate and explain to the house and the people of this country her reasons for wanting it changed. Let us hear what these people are going to say, if anything.
Some time, Mr. Speaker-I will not say when-there will be a vote on this subamendment. It provides for a reference of the matter to the people of Canada and, as I stated previously, it leaves room for the inclusion of other designs. Let the people decide. That, surely, is non-contentious. What is wrong with that? If our hon. friends opposite think they are right, why do they not let the people decide? They say, "It is our duty to do it". Nothing could be further from the truth. In the apparent arrogant refusal of most members on the government side of the house to participate in this debate we see the ultimate in political irresponsibility.
Hear, hear.

The
people of this country may not remember much of what we say there, but they will never forget that most hon. members opposite said nothing. A few days ago we listened with attention and respect to the speech of the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto). His speech placed emphasis on this particular point. Among other things, he said:
We on this side have wondered how it is that so many people in Canada are staunchly entrenched behind the red ensign, a fact we did not expect, people who would otherwise have fondly and readily welcomed a new distinctive flag. It is because they are afraid, and have gathered under the ensign in fear and apprehension of one thing-the division of this nation. They fear the division and separatism about which they have heard.
Canadian Flag
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for York East expresses as a fact that they fear and apprehend a division of the nation. I say that the hon. member has brought to the attention of this house a most important point and one that deserves a tremendous amount of thought and consideration by every responsible member, because it suggests in its language that when people are fearful and apprehensive about their nation, and subsequently about themselves, their families and the future of their families, they seek comfort and protection in something that has come down through the years, because it is one of those things they need in the circumstances I have just described.
So what do they do? They reach for the red ensign. Those are the words of the hon. member for York East and they are also my sentiments, Mr. Speaker. I emphasize that they are the words that hon. member uttered in this chamber, because he said that when people fear something and are afraid the country will be divided, they reach for the red ensign-which means something to them and is an emblem that has come down through the years.
Hear, hear.

And
Mr. Speaker, this is the symbol this government proposes to scrap, discard, and destroy. Yet the hon. member for York East very properly points out that in his opinion the symbol for which people reach is the red ensign. Where could you find a better, more potent argument for the retention of the red ensign and the things for which it stands? It has been many times tried, never denied, and willing to be tried again.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I believe the hon. member deserves the commendation of this house for the point he has brought out and the opinion he has expressed concerning the unity of the nation, even though I find it difficult to believe in his conclusion, which was that he would support the government sponsored design. Yet I recognize his concern for national unity and express my own similar concern. Where we differ to a tremendous extent is with regard to the means we think are necessary to bring about that unity.
So we have the union jack as one of the symbols with regard to which we seek authority to vote, and I do not need to emphasize its significance.
It is the emblem of liberty, truth and justice. Who is there here willing to do away with his rights to justice as a citizen

Canadian Flag
of this country? No one. Liberty and truth are also important words in the lives of each and every one of us.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on but my time is nearly up. My last words in these few remarks are simply these. It seems to me that this question may and can be solved if only it is approached in a proper state of mind and with a proper attitude. Let us forget what constitutes a political advantage of a temporary nature and remember that the eyes of Canada are on what this parliament does in connection with this most important matter. If we have a few days on other business and then return, this might be a proper course to consider. But in my concluding remarks I deny once more the urgency of the matter. This matter is not urgent. It would be much better to resolve it in a proper way, so that this nation will go forward united, in the years to come, than to tell us that we must resolve it in a week or two and in the wrong way. Those, Mr. Speaker, are my concluding remarks.

Mr. Speaker, in rising today to take part in this debate, may I say that, like the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) I too spoke on July 3 and at that time expressed my personal views on this resolution. However I feel it would be proper that I put on record the views and opinions of many of the people who have written me in regard to this subject.
Before commencing to put these views on record I would again emphasize that the statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) on behalf of the government, that the reason the government are trying to expedite this issue is because of an election promise is ridiculous. It only proves once more the inefficiency of the government in planning and preparing legislation. In this way they are trying to conceal their inability and inefficiency. To prove that the Prime Minister said the reason for this issue being brought up at this time is that it was an election promise. I should like to refer back to last August 25, when a question was asked of the Postmaster General with regard to a statement attributed to the minister of northern affairs in the last election campaign. The Postmaster General replied that these statements were just election promises and did not carry any authenticity-in other words, that they would not hold any water. I might add that this promise was only made in chosen spots in Canada.

For no other reason than to persuade the government to turn down the resolution, I would invite them to visit the city of Peterborough. In front of the J. J. Turner works, manufacturers of flags, there are three flags, the union jack, the red ensign and the proposed maple leaf flag. These flags were mounted at the same time, and I would invite any hon. member of this house or any citizen to go to Peterborough and observe the three flags flying there today. Sir, the new proposed flag is a filthy, dirty brownish colour.
Oh, oh.
Hon. members can say "oh, oh", but if they are interested they can drive down to Peterborough, where they can see it for themselves. The other flags have retained their beauty.
Made by another manufacturer.

I should like to refer to a statement by the Rev. Gordon Smyth in a sermon delivered in the Parkdale United Church in Ottawa. He said:
It is impossible to cut symbolism out of the affairs of men and nations; the roots go too deep. If a man were to resolve never to use a symbol again he could not shake hands with a friend, put a ring on the finger of his bride, kiss his child or take the sacrament. Human nature requires symbols. The heart craves after some tangible expression of the intangible. The mind is ill at ease until it casts into a material form something of the mysterious emotions of the soul.
May I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned at the dinner hour I was endeavouring to put on record the views of many Canadians from all walks of life who have written to me. However, during the supper hour I could not help thinking how grateful and appreciative many members on the opposite side of the house are, or should be, to this party for taking the stand that we have not or will not let the Prime Minister or government railroad or bulldoze this legislation through.
Having known personally many of the members on the opposite side of the house I am aware of some of their views and opinions. Sir, many of them are of the same opinion

as we are on this side. However, Mr. Speaker, those members have been lucky. They are not muzzled because they are vicious, but because the front benchers know of their views and what the outcome would be if they expressed themselves. They know that the outcome would be detrimental to the government. Time and time again our members have requested members opposite to speak on this resolution.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member says "oh". I would class him in the same category as that hon. member who announced today in Montreal that he is not going to attend the House of Commons again, but will boycott it until such time as the flag resolution is passed.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. I would not like the hon. member to classify me in any way, except as a real Canadian who wants to have a flag as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I was classifying the hon. member with one of the members of his party who made a statement in Montreal today. I am glad to hear the hon. member say that he is a real Canadian. We are all looking forward to hearing his speech on this issue.
You have asked me a question and I will answer it right away.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer again to the hon. member who made a statement in Montreal today, and suggest that he is neglecting his duty, which is to be in attendance in this house to present his views on the flag issue rather than to make statements to the press to the effect he is going to stay home and boycott the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, you will remember the embarrassing position in which many members were placed when this resolution was introduced. I well remember the week end that members were instructed to scurry back to their ridings and attempt to pacify their constituents. I also remember when they returned to this house they did so with their tails between their legs, because the constituents had told them what they thought. Since that time they have been embarrassed.
I know where you come from.

The hon. member is making his usual contribution to this house.

Give them hell, Moe.

The hon. member says he knows where I come from, Mr. Speaker. God only knows that there is no one any more proud of his heritage than I, and that is something the hon. member cannot say.
Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was quoting from a statement by the Rev. Gordon Smyth. I should now like to carry on with that statement, which reads as follows:
Why, then, Is the Issue of our national symbols so explosive? Because it has not been set in the context of the significance of religion, alike in history and modern life. The fundamental importance of religion in the development of the human race may be more clearly recognized if we consider certain possible divergences from history... Let us suppose that Christianity had remained a racial sect. Let us suppose that Charles Martel had failed against the Mohammedans at the Battle of the Pyrenees. Let us suppose that French missionaries had not shared the lot of settlers along the shores of the St. Lawrence. Let us suppose that saddle-bag ministers of the gospel had not helped to bring law and order, education and courage to English speaking Upper Canada. Let us suppose that the Fathers of Confederation had brought to their conferences only shrewd, practical, bargaining points, with no spirit touched by common allegiance to the founder of Christianity...
And yet Canadians cannot afford to be either smug or complacent. Too many spurn the lessons of the past. Too many echo the pernicious sentiment that "whatever is, is right." Too many fail to realize that to believe in "the easy buck" or "the mood of the voters" is a disastrous philosophy which, in the long run, catches up with them. Too many are unable to accept the facts of history because, unlike citizens of other nations, they no longer know those facts.
Such a statement from a child just may be understandable. But what of a deputy minister of citizenship and immigration who recently referred me to his office since he was not sure what Victoria day is called nowadays?
All this has a bearing on the explosive issue of national symbols. It would appear that anything goes, provided it goes. That is just a point. Anything just does not go from the long term point of view. The Americans learned this the hard way in the civil war over the federal power versus state rights 100 years ago. Shades of trends in Canada. Latterly I have been discussing the matter with numerous English speaking members of parliament.
I would commend this to many members opposite.
They are practically of one accord. They are frustrated. They are pessimistic. They privately resent the fact that while French Canadians vigorously assert their right to symbols of their own, they would seemingly deny a similar right to

Canadian Flag
meaningful symbols for the nation as a whole by seeking to rub the federal slate clean of 'the British connection'. They keenly resent all this privately and yet most of them publicly proclaim "peace, peace" when actually there is less and less peace. "The voice of English Canada is silent", they say sadly. They fail to add that this includes their own voices. This is not healthy. It is the symptom of a dread disease.
This is a major lesson out of the past. The past! Permit me to quote from a statement by Dr. Eugene Forsey who requires no introduction to people acquainted with public affairs. Exclaims Dr. Forsey:
"This government is firmly committed to the basically bicultural character of our country, yet it proposes a flag which contains not the slightest reference to any culture whatever, even agriculture. If the country is basically bicultural, then the flag should be basically bicultural too. Everything human, every vestige of our history, everything distinctively Canadian, except a piece of vegetation, has been carefully excluded."
Of course, it is realized that Canadians have carried the insignia of the maple leaf on their uniforms in time of war. However, this has been played up out of all proportion. The Royal Canadian Legion knows this. What segment of the population is in a better position to know? What segment deserves as much respect? Those whom we call veterans wore the maple leaf but they did not follow the maple leaf into battle. They followed ideals symbolized by the union jack and the Canadian red ensign. I have a notion that if they have gone on record as favouring the parliamentary definition of the ensign as the national flag this is not to rub the noses of French Canadians in the victory of General James Wolfe on the plains of Abraham but rather to affirm those precious elements in both cultures which we have in common.
What is the common denominator? Not something taken from nature, but from human nature. Not just maple leaves from trees found on this continent outside of Canada as well as inside our borders, but a human, living symbol unique in our particular part of the western hemisphere. I refer to the monarchy. I have in mind the crown. I have in mind that crown which Sir Georges Etienne Cartier extolled as the protector of the rights of French Canadians and which Sir Wilfrid Laurier extolled time and again. Are there English Canadians who feel that this symbol is outmoded? Are there French Canadians who feel that this symbol is merely an Anglo-Saxon emblem of superiority?
I do not doubt it. Unfortunately it would appear so. I have even been told by a parliamentary expert in heraldry that a crown above the cluster of maple leaves on the proposed flag would not be suitable from the heraldic standpoint. This expert stated that by the same standard the stars and stripes would fail to get a pass mark. Tell that to the average American! Moreover, the broadcast indication that a special banner may be prepared, with the union jack and the crown for commonwealth occasions, is little more than a sop. You had a request this afternoon to make a speech, so your turn is coming.
Never was there a juncture in national affairs like the present crisis to spark a grasp of what the Right Hon. Vincent Massey said out of his far flung knowledge of this land in the capacity of governor general. In his book entitled "On Being Canadian" Mr. Massey has written: "The supreme contribution to the cause of our unity is made by the crown. Nothing else with us stands above all controversy, represents equally all the elements which make up the state and preserves the vital factor of continuity in our national life." The wisdom of these words should be superimposed above the popularity of maple leaves on our proposed national flag. The alternative is even greater division. The omission of this symbol will result in the sort of natural protest and feeling of injustice in many parts of Canada which many in Quebec still manifest toward a certain political party over the conscription issue of 1917.
May I say in passing that at lunch hour a gentleman spoke to me who had just returned last evening from a tour through Quebec. He said he had seen as many red ensigns flying in Quebec as any other flag and I say, thank God for that.
The omission of this symbol will cause the Canadian red ensign to continue to be flown over the legislative buildings and institutions of a majority of the provinces from Newfoundland to British Columbia.
It is with this prediction, this warning, in mind that I quote from the Kingston Whig-Standard. The Whig-Standard can hardly be branded as either a Progressive Conservative or socialist newspaper. The fact of the matter is that its president, Hon. W. Rupert Davies, is a Liberal senator in the upper house. A recent editorial in that newspaper dealt in no uncertain terms with the flag issue. To millions of Canadians the union jack is a symbol of everything worth while in life. Even more serious is the fact that, in rejecting the union jack, we are rejecting the symbol of that special relationship to God given to nations which officially acknowledge Him by using His Cross as

their emblem. Further, in a world of turmoil and aggression, we lose the protection which that relationship provides.
The three crosses, as arranged on the union jack, form the first and the last letters of the ancient Hebrew alphabet (Sinai script). Thus, by rejecting the union jack we are not only repudiating that special relationship to God which is our birthright, but are taking ourselves out from under the protection of His name into the appalling dangers of the coming Armageddon.
Only Satan can gain anything from such incredible folly.
Who is the author of that?
The Toronto district branch of the Canadian British-Israel association.
Your friends, Bert.

The reason I know the cross-sectional ferment among the people over the flag, and the disgust and discouragement with parliament, guilty or innocent, is because my professional income must be supplemented by wide commercial travel.

In closing, may I say we know that the Prime Minister has been misled. We realize that he has been misled by some of his advisers; but it is not too late for him to change his ways. Responsibility for this debate rests with the other side of the house. All they have to do, over there, is withdraw their resolution and the debate will be at an end. If this were done, no one would know how anyone in a certain section of the country had voted, or how the majority of votes had gone in a particular area. We do not want to know how people in a particular part of the country voted. We want to know how Canadians as a whole voted. We want a united Canada, and that is what we are fighting for.

It had
not been my intention to take part in this debate, but I think the house will be interested in a few observations at this point from one who takes an objective view of contentious issues.

I have just returned from a ten day visit to my constituency where I had the opportunity to meet a good number of my constituents. I am always interested in finding out what the average person is thinking in relation to what is happening in parliament. I have discussed this flag issue with a good many people. I must say that my conversations clearly indicated that the soundest way in which to settle this matter would be by means of a plebiscite.
I wanted to find out how public opinion was reflected in other ways, so I went into a number of stores and asked: Are you selling the Prime Minister's flag? And on every occasion they said: What do you think; do you think I want to go bankrupt? I cannot find this design being sold anywhere. That is the situation as I found it in my constituency.
I returned to Ottawa during the latter part of last week and I must say I was somewhat surprised, after a little investigation, to find a situation existing here in Ottawa which further confirmed the opinion I have expressed previously in this debate, that the only fair way to settle this matter was through a national plebiscite. I suggest that such a plebiscite could be held at the time of the next general election at which point persons would have an opportunity to express their opinions on this matter. I suggest that if it were put to them at such a plebiscite the great majority of the Canadian people would willingly accept the decision. We are all democrats, although at times when I look across the other side of the house I have my doubts.
Some two months ago, when this flag was first introduced and the model first flown on parliament hill and on the flagstaff of the Prime Minister's residence, naturally there were persons who were interested in purchasing flags and selling them. At that time, the sale price in Ottawa was $1. That was the general price. I went and inquired of the joke shop on Bank street, which was selling quite a few. Now that the debate has gone on for some while, and people have had an opportunity to think this matter over, what has happened? Since my return, I have inquired how the flags are selling and I find that the price had dropped to 79 cents. Then, later they dropped to 59 cents. At the conclusion of the exhibition, I found that a gentleman who had a store there was trying to get rid of them for 19 cents. Mr. Speaker, I think this clearly indicates a growing lack of interest in the flag proposed by the Prime Minister even in the capital city.

I respect anyone's point of view, but I say this is a good indication of the necessity for giving the Canadian people the opportunity to express opinions on this matter. After all, in the capital city a great deal has been done to support the Prime Minister's flag. I believe he has had the support of a good many individuals in more or less indirect ways. On this account I would urge the right hon. gentleman to accept the proposal put forward by the opposition, that a national plebiscite be held so that the Canadian people may themselves decide this important issue which goes beyond the realm of economics and beyond the realm of legislation of other types; it strikes to the roots of the people's loyalties and sentiments. The Canadian people should be given the opportunity to decide for themselves the Canadian flag they wish to have in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate at the invitation of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) I make no apology. Had the flag been an election issue and a plank in the Liberal platform during the election of 1963, whereby the people of Canada could have expressed their views, I would have taken a different viewpoint. Since it was not, except, as one would surmise, that possibly a different front was presented to our French speaking Canadians in Quebec than was presented to the other nine provinces in Canada, I feel it my duty to speak on behalf of the constituents of my riding and express their views and ardent desire -to maintain the red ensign.
The introduction of the amendment and subamendment are the only possible opportunities accorded members to voice their opinions. I have a letter sent by the dean of Mount Royal College, Calgary, Alberta, to the hon. member for London (Mr. Irvine), and I am going to read a short excerpt from it:
While I was in New York this summer, I was asked to address a group on "Education in Canada". In order to refresh my memory I went down to

Canadian Flag
the Canadian consul's office at 680 Fifth avenue, (9th floor, I believe) for a bit of information. They gave me an envelope which they call a teacher's kit. This contains a large political map of Canada; speeches of prominent Canadians, (e.g. Lester Pearson, Paul Martin, Paul Hellyer, Walter Gordon);-
I do not see the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) or the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) listed here:
-a booklet, summarizing the geography, climate, etc., of Canada; and a thicker booklet giving all sorts of facts about the country; and a Canadian flag (enclosed). It is to be noted that this is described as "distinctive of Canada".
The brochure enclosed with the letter is entitled "The Canadian Red Ensign" and it
says:
The flag now used as distinctive of Canada is properly described as the red ensign with the shield of the coat of arms of Canada in the fly. The flag consists of a red field, with the union jack in the first quarter, next to the staff. The inclusion of the union jack signifies Canada's association with the other members of the British commonwealth of nations. The coat of arms bears the emblems of the four countries from which the original settlers of Canada were chiefly drawn- the three lions of England, the lilies of France, the lion rampant of Scotland and the harp of Ireland-together with a branch carrying three maple leaves, the special emblem of Canada.
The Canadian red ensign may be flown from buildings owned or occupied by the Canadian government within or without Canada.
It is also appropriate for the Canadian ensign to be flown within or without Canada wherever place or occasion may make it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag.
It is indication enough, when this kind of brochure is put out in the United States, that this government did think the red ensign was a distinctive Canadian flag. I have received all kinds of petitions, copies of which have been sent to the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne). They are addressed to the Secretary of State of Canada and are headed:
We the undersigned respectfully request the Canadian red ensign, which has been authorized by four governments of Canada during the past 70 years by order in council P.C. 5888 and signed by the Governor General on September 5, 1945, be retained as the flag of Canada.
It is very interesting to look over the names that appear on the petitions. Evidence that this was not an election promise in my riding during the last election campaign is clearly indicated by a signature here of one of the nominees at the Liberal convention, and another name is that of one of the Liberal organizers in my area. There are also a good many other names which indicate that these people did not expect this issue to be initiated by the government.

The announcement-or, I should say, the political speech-made by the Prime Minister at the dominion Legion convention at Winnipeg was very ill advised and controversial, being given in the memorial ritual opening ceremonies. I happened to be in Winnipeg for that convention and my personal feeling was that he was very ill advised to make a political speech and try to choke the Legion members with the new proposed flag. Had it been debated on the floor of the convention the legionnaires would have taken a much different attitude. One thing this government has failed to recognize, I would say, being a veteran myself, is that 70 per cent of the supporters of this government are legionnaires; and not only that, but the armed services are pretty strong supporters of the government. It is very surprising to me that they would consider killing the hen that laid the golden egg.
I have many telegrams here. To mention only a few, there is one from C. C. Sparling, the dominion president of the Legion. This telegram reads:
The Royal Canadian Legion at its 20th biennial convention in Winnipeg overwhelmingly endorses the Canadian red ensign and asks your unqualified support of its stand.
I also have a telegram from the outgoing provincial president of the Ontario command of the Legion, which reads:
Dominion convention Royal Canadian Legion Winnipeg May 21st approved Canadian red ensign as Legion's official flag to be flown over all Legion branches and commands now and in future. Ontario command 525 branches and 86,000 members request your consideration in support of Canadian red ensign at time of vote in parliament on flag question.
That is signed by A. H. Adams, president, Ontario command, Royal Canadian Legion.
I also have a telegram from the zone commander in my own district, J. H. Hackett, which reads:
Zone II wishes your support in maintaining red ensign.
I also have a letter from practically every branch in the riding of the ladies auxiliary and the Canadian corps, all asking for support of the red ensign. I have letters from the women's auxiliaries, the I.O.D.E., the Canadian-British Israel association of Ontario, and women's institutes. This represents a large voice of the people of Canada, and their feeling is that the Canadian red ensign should be maintained.
I should like to quote a letter from a nationally known figure, a veteran of the last war and a man who has done a great deal

for crippled children in Canada. I am sure he is known by all hon. members. I refer to Conn Smythe of Toronto. He says:
The enclosed article is both interesting and informative.
The article to which he refers is entitled "Symbol of Unity" and is taken from the Veterans Advocate of August, 1963. The letter continues:
The red ensign has been authorized as our flag by four governments of Canada during the past 70 years, the latest being by order in council (P.C. 5888) September 5, 1945.
The statement that our flag is not distinctive is, to say the least, erroneous. There can be no doubt in the minds of the Cypriots, Greeks and Turks, when they see the Van Doos and the red ensign, as to where these troops come from.
In the Olympic games the whole world is represented and when Canada sometimes wins a gold medal everybody knows, when the red ensign is raised to the masthead, that Canada has won a world's championship.
With the continued world-wide success of Canada as a country, and the extraordinary individual feats of Canadians under this flag, it might not be amiss to wonder who or what is behind this movement to haul down our flag. We should be on our guard that we as Canadians are not being led up the garden path.
I will read part of this statement entitled "Symbol of Unity", but may I first mention the editor's footnote. The article is by Brigadier Ian S. Johnston, C.B.E., D.S.O., E.D.; chevalier, legion of honour; croix de guerre, and the footnote is: "Here is the most mature and thoughtful presentation on a Canadian flag which has appeared during the prolonged, needless controversy. It is worth reading no matter what personal views you hold". This statement reads, in part:
Canada now has 19 million people, but over two million of them are not native born. It means a serious leavening problem for the assimilation is complicated by our growing pains, but Canada is in fact a country with an honourable past where the problems of religious and racial differences have already been resolved. Canadians have developed a greater tolerance than we perhaps ourselves realize.
Few factors could be more effective in fostering and enhancing this than a thoughtful appraisal of the elements embodied in the Canadian ensign, which has played the role of our official Canadian flag since before the Kaiser war.
When its design is examined dispassionately without prejudice or unreasoned emotion, it can be seen that every desire of our multiple religious, racial and cultural backgrounds is answered.
If we aspire to religious and racial tolerance and the attainment of our national objective by negotiation, while maintaining loyalty to ideals rather than narrow nationalism, then our Canadian ensign represents us in a manner that no simple combination of colours or numbers could do.
Canadian Flag
A flag with great depth of meaning capable of representing our complex idealism, it also represents our varied traditions and cultures, but single aspiration of the Canadian people as a whole, in a manner which a new design could not possibly match.
By understanding the ensign through a study of the elements in the flag, we may better understand ourselves, and will see that all of us proclaim it as our symbol of unity, the ideal flag for a country like ours. ...
A flag should be emblematic of its people, and this is clearly achieved. ...
Why is this group of devices called an "ensign" rather than a flag? A flag is a piece of cloth used for signalling or other purposes such as denoting danger, surrender, pestilence or all clear. An ensign may be a flag or other device, but it has the special function of denoting identity and is a rallying point. In our case it is interesting to note that the word is derived through the French word "enseigne".
The very complexity of our flag is a virtue. It represents ideals, and ideals are not simple matters. Here is a flag that has wealth of meaning and inspiration for each one of us according to our bent. A true student of heraldry can discover in it far more than is suggested above.
The people who own to this flag are the independant sons of the partnership of great peoples. The religious and racial tolerances we represent were achieved only at great cost.
While we negotiate, we do so only with honour and remain loyal to the death to our ideals. If civilization is to survive Canada must cherish her spirit of brotherhood, and lead the way against narrow nationalism.
Twice, without hesitation, our young men have fought under this flag and given their lives for the righteous cause against narrow nationalism.
Our interest is the common good, the brotherhood of man-a modern concept to be achieved only in a country held in reserve by the Creator for just such a people.
This is what we are-that is what our ensign proclaims us to be.

This article reads:
The Commons summer recess has gone the way that seems to afflict Victoria's summer weather; there won't be any. Having got its interim supply bill through at last, and for three months instead of two, parliament will sit well into the fall.
The assumption is that the Commons will then recess and prepare for a new session. That is, once Mr. Pearson has rammed his new flag into the statute books. He acts like a schoolmaster

who won't let his form go home until it bows to his wishes.
In the present impasse that hamstrings parliament and sees it sitting through the hot months of an eastern summer the prime Minister displays the petulance so often associated with persons of weak character. He seems to imagine that a show of authority is an indication of strength, even when a diplomatic way out of the dilemma is offered him.
Where does the blame for the present parliamentary stalemate lie? Solely in Mr. Pearson's obduracy over the flag issue. This is the core that keeps parliament sitting and the normal business of the country held back from speedy progression.
This has been evident ever since he introduced the flag resolution. To begin with he held the threat of an election over M.P.'s heads, did they fail to pass the flag measure, which was tantamount to holding a gun at their heads and depriving them of unbiased decision.
In fact, the long sitting hours are just another indication of the same thing.
He refused a free vote on the subject. While blaming Mr. Diefenbaker for non-compliance he has now prevented the compromise suggestion that would delay the contentious flag bill to a fall session by insisting on an unacceptable time limit to its debate.
It is not obstructionism on the part of Mr. Diefenbaker that is at fault but the Prime Minister's insistence on having his own way.
Mr. Pearson says he is not prepared to call an election on any of the current issues facing parliament, the flag of course being the main one. Is he afraid of the result? This would probably be the quickest and most salutary solution to a parliamentary stalemate that grows worse with each passing day.
The country has been told that an election would split it and create national disunity. The lack of unity presently so evident in relation to Quebec dissidence and to the question of a new flag could not be greater. An election in fact would dear the air by either giving Mr. Pearson a majority mandate, and thus enabling national acceptance of his policies, the flag included, or rejecting his regime in toto.
But Mr. Pearson is bent on following his own stubborn course, although one wonders how much longer the smaller opposition groups can abide such intractability and the debilitating and unsatisfactory situation thus forced on parliament. The former U.N. diplomat of high repute certainly reveals his feet of clay. Stubbornship is no substitute for statesmanship.
This is a democratic country and the only way it can continue to be democratic is by our exercising our freedom of speech in this house. I hear the word "filibuster" used continually lately, but I think it dates back quite a bit to before the commencement of the flag debate. [Mr. Madill.l
headed: "Peel representative explains filibuster", and I will only put on record a short extract:
Flaws in Canada's parliamentary system came to light early last week when one opposition party proved it could bring parliament to a standstill. In an obvious move to delay debate on the flag issue, it entered into a speech making marathon on the type of business that does not call for a vote on specific issues: interim supply.
I could not help but notice that when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) made his speech it reeked of the word "filibuster".
Mr. Speaker, at a time just before we normally would have taken Easter recess, simply because the hon. member for Edmon-ton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) stood for his rights in this house and objected to a bill involving $140 million being passed without debate, three of our hon. friends to the left in the New Democratic party spoke continuously. Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question? Would he explain to the house why the Conservatives are speaking at a time when we are waiting to settle two Conservative amendments?

For one reason, we are waiting to hear your speeches. If you were listening to my earlier remarks you would have heard me say that we are speaking at the invitation of the Prime Minister.
Getting back to the subamendment, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote a portion of an article written by Charles Lynch which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on August 22. You probably will not want to hear this either, but Mr. Lynch states:
The red ensign is now stronger than ever.
If not above the battle, it at least flew over the battlefield-and its position seems considerably stronger at summer's end than it was at the beginning.

In terms of the House of Commons, it has been an effective political manoeuvre.
Whether it has been as effective in terms of the country remains to be seen.

Mr. Speaker, had the flag been sent to a committee at the beginning and a free vote given to hon. members I am reasonably sure the flag debate would have been concluded. This is another occasion of the cart being placed before the horse or, shall I say, another case of trial and error.
The hon. member for London (Mr. Irvine) offered constructive criticism the other day, and I think he made a worth-while contribution when he suggested that a committee should select several flags and present them to the country for a choice, and that no government would stand or fall on this issue.
