We certainly would not want this type of debate to commence every time the government changed.
As a veteran I feel strongly in support of the red ensign, and I intend to maintain that position even though I would compromise in order to maintain the unity in this country which is vital to each and every one of us sent here by our constituents.
An article appeared in the Toronto Telegram on August 22, which sums up the situation very well, and I think it is worth quoting for the record. The article begins:
Ask the people.
The Canadian ensign must not be lowered without the consent of the people.
No decision of the House of Commons, by free vote or otherwise, to strike our historic ensign and replace it with a pennant of the Prime Minister's choosing can be construed as expressing the consensus of the nation.
The voice of the people can be heard, on this issue, only through a national plebiscite.
None would seriously suggest that all controversial issues before parliament should be resolved by plebiscite or referendum. That is not the way our system works. A government having received its mandate, pushes ahead with its legislative program and stakes its life on its success or failure.
But the flag issue is different.
Here is a matter that touches the hearts, the emotions, the loyalties of virtually all Canadians. A parliamentary vote that would destroy the country's flag would leave deep and festering scars for years to come.
Too big for compromise.
It is far too important to be settled by parliamentary compromise.
Though Prime Minister Pearson has given extraordinary priority to the flag legislation, he did not
Canadian Flag
make it a central part of his campaign when he was seeking election. True, he promised a new flag within two years.
There was no suggestion that parliament would be presented with a single, peculiar pennant design and be told that this must be our flag.
If there had been such a proposition, it is quite possible that Mr. Pearson's minority representation in the House of Commons would have been considerably smaller.
It has been said that a plebiscite would be divisive. This is nonsense. Nothing could have been more divisive than the Prime Minister's introduction of the issue as a matter of high priority.
By doing so, he has made the national flag a partisan political issue. If he succeeds in forcing it on the country, it will be looked upon by thousands of Canadians as a political badge. It will fail to receive the honour and respect that belongs now to the ensign.
Mr. Pearson, as an act of compromise, has announced that he would allow a free vote; that is, individual members would be allowed to vote as they like outside the discipline of their parties.
This is a move in the right direction-or, it would have been had it been made earlier.
Vote can't be free.
At this stage, with party lines hardened, it is difficult to conceive of a truly free vote.
Having shown, belatedly, a willingness to retreat from his earlier stubborn demands for the banner of his choice, he now should go one step further and measure public sentiment by plebiscite.
Perhaps Mr. Pearson fears the outcome of such a testing of public opinion. Letters and petitions expressing determination to retain the ensign have been impressive.
There is no reason why this obstructive and divisive bill should not be shelved pending a reference to the people. There is no urgency. Most Canadians outside Quebec appear to be quite satisfied with the flag we have now. In Quebec, the matter is of little importance as there they fly the Laurentian flag with its white cross and fleur-de-lis.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member has been reading for the last four or five minutes an editorial in toto. I suggest hon. members may make references to editorials but should make their own speeches in this effort at filibuster.

I could do that, but I think perhaps what I am doing is hurting the hon. members' toes worse than if I made my own speech. Mr. Speaker, I am almost finished, and I will then be glad to listen to that hon. member read or make a speech, however distasteful.
The article I was reading continues:
Until Mr. Pearson softens his stand, the opposition is justified in continuing a modified filibuster. As distasteful as such devices are in parliament, no other method seems practical in the face of Mr. Pearson's stubbornness.
The way out of the parliamentary impasse is clear; a plebiscite to end the long debate and to allow parliament to get on with more important legislation.

Canadian Flag
I have one further comment to make, Mr. Speaker. I hope a Canadian flag means more to that hon. member sitting on the opposite side than a symbol on a bathing skirt, or a sticker on a bumper. The Canadian flag means something more than that to me, and I hope it means more to the hon. member. Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to bring before this house the feeling of the majority of people in my constituency. This is the first time I have spoken during the flag debate, and I have no apology to make for taking up the time of this house. I feel that every member of this house should speak during this debate.
I should like to say a word or two about the speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp). I feel he should be congratulated because he is the first cabinet minister to speak on the flag issue. I think we should hear more from cabinet ministers if they feel so strongly about the three maple leaves design. The minister accused the Conservative party of carrying on a filibuster, and I should like to read from the beginning of his remarks. As found on page 6956 of Hansard he said:
Mr. Speaker, I have hestltated to take part In this debate, not from any lack of conviction but because no one with respect for our parliamentary institutions would wish to contribute to the filibuster now under way.
I do not believe this was his true feeling, for later in his speech he said, as found on page 6961:
During the last few days I have made a point of listening to the speeches made in this debate both on the subamendment and on the amendment which is still before the house... I must say that all those to whom I listened spoke with great sincerity. They stated with sincerity their convictions about a Canadian flag, and this is as it should be. X have no quarrel with that.
Why did he start his speech by accusing this party of a filibuster? I feel he was sincere in his speech and I believe that everybody who has spoken in this debate has been sincere. Everyone knows that when the Prime Minister introduced the flag resolution he expressed the hope that everyone wishing to speak on it would be able to do so. Yet every time he comes in the house he accuses us of a filibuster. The majority of the people in nine of the provinces do not feel it is a filibuster, nor do I think the people in the province of Quebec feel it is a filibuster.
I agree that no party should obstruct the business of the house. I also agree that no one man should tell this country what flag
[Mr. Madill.l
we are going to fly for the next generation, for our children and their children. I do not think that one man should get up in the house, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) did, and criticize any other member and any other party. Since I have been a member of the house I think he and his party have certainly used more of parliament's time than the party I represent.
I do not believe that any member of the house should ask for closure, as the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Mar-coux) did several days ago. I should like to ask the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) if he supports this view, but I see he is not in the house at present. I should also like to ask the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) whether he supports closure. In this regard I should like to quote from a memorandum that he sent to his constituents in which he said:
The people of Canada have never heen asked nor have the people said they want a new flag other than the red ensign. The chief electoral officer should be notified that the opinion of the people is necessary to settle the matter and, therefore, should proceed to have a vote taken by way of a transferable ballot on which a number of choice designs, including the red ensign, are manifest.
It is a two page memorandum and it is very interesting. I wonder whether the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency read it before he made his speech.
To go back to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I should like to compliment him because he said he would not support closure or any action of that type in the house. But I should like to point out the fact that he claimed it made his blood boil when people spoke disparagingly about the three maple leaves. How does he think the people who support the red ensign feel when they see the Liberal government trying to tear down the red ensign? The minister says we need a spirit of tolerance, and I say to the minister that is what the Conservative party is asking the government for. We are asking them to show tolerance in choosing a flag for Canada. While the minister was speaking he left me with the impression that he felt only the Liberal government could bring in a flag for Canada. I say that if the flag resolution had been presented to the house properly the country would never have been divided on this issue.
The Ottawa Journal summed up the question of the flag in an editorial in today's issue when it said that the real task is to produce

a flag that will unite the nation, and that whether this takes a month or four months is relatively unimportant. My correspondence has consisted of several hundred letters in favour of the retention of the red ensign and only six letters in favour of the new maple leaf flag. I have a letter here from a lady who has asked me to support the three maple leaves. She lost her only son in the last war and her brother in the first war. I appreciate letters of this type, but for this one letter I have received 100 letters asking for the retention of the red ensign. Many of the letters I have received supporting the red ensign intimate that the writers would be willing to accept a modified version of the ensign, if this is what is needed to unite Canada; but in most cases they point out very emphatically that they cannot accept the new flag proposed by the Prime Minister. This is a good reason why we should have a plebiscite or a committee set up to consider the flag.
Since the flag resolution was proposed to the house we find that all across the nation people are showing an interest in the Canadian red ensign that has never been shown before. Red ensigns are now being flown from private homes, factories and other places of business, and cottages. When I go home on the week end I sometimes have a chance to go to the lake and every cottage is flying a red ensign or a maple leaf flag. There is another member in the house who has a cottage on the lake and he has been flying the one maple leaf flag. Two or three weeks ago the flag was taken down, but when I went there last Sunday he had it flying at half mast. So I do not know what to expect next week. It might be the red ensign, and I hope it will be.
The hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. Webb) referred earlier this evening to the flag manufacturer in Peterborough. This is an old, established firm which has been doing business throughout the dominion for years. In the last four months this firm has sold as many red ensigns and union jacks as it did in the previous five or six years. This is further proof that the house should be very careful before it selects a national emblem. We need an emblem that will unite us. We need an emblem that will evoke respect, loyalty, affection, an emblem of which all Canadians will be proud. Most Canadians feel that the red ensign has accomplished this, but I know these people are willing to compromise in order to have unity in the country. If the majority of members of the house feel that we need a new distinctive
Canadian Flag
Canadian flag I believe that if they are sincere they will ask for a plebiscite or for the setting up of a committee to design a flag acceptable to all.
Speaking in this house last week the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) asked the government to consider a design that would represent the English and French population as well as the rest of Canada. Designs of this type should be considered. The house must come up with a design that will unite the country, not one that is going to divide it. His was a very interesting speech and I would like to quote one paragraph from it:
That is why we are exerting so much pressure and making these requests. We beg our colleagues of the Liberal party to exert pressure on the Prime Minister to set up a committee to choose a design which, as I said, would, unite and not divide the country, in short, knit together into one unit all the elements of our country.
I believe this is the feeling of the people in Quebec today. The flag proposed by the Prime Minister is certainly not acceptable to the majority of people in Canada. If Quebec chooses to be represented by the maple leaf or fleur-de-lis, and I respect them for that, the rest of Canada should have a choice as to their symbol. As confederation approaches its 100th birthday we realize across the country that we need Quebec and that the province of Quebec needs the rest of Canada if each province is to prosper and progress.
Last week I had a family from Detroit, Michigan, visit me in the house and they listened to the flag debate. Later on in my office their nine year old son said to me, "Mr. Stenson, we could solve the flag debate for you. You join our country and we will put another star on our flag for you". If this should ever come to pass, and I hope it never does, it will wipe out all the tradition and culture of our country. Canada certainly does not want to give up its heritage and traditions, for if it does confederation would be meaningless.
As we approach the centennial year and the world fair in Montreal, we find we have a selling job on our hands, to sell this fair across our country. But if the Prime Minister thinks the new flag will promote unity and sell the fair to Canada, he is very much mistaken. This feeling has been growing in the last few months. Let's not let it get out of hand because it is not fair to the province of Quebec: it is not fair to the rest of Canada. Let the house set up a committee which could bring forward suggestions for a flag- four or five designs-and then let the people

Canadian Flag
pick their flag by a plebiscite so that they will feel they have had a part in picking their design, as is proper in a democracy.
Our Prime Minister has turned a deaf ear on the Royal Canadian Legion of Canada. Although not a veteran myself I feel I have a responsibility to the veterans in my constituency and to every Legion branch across Canada. Can we forget so easily that since 1914 over one million men and women fought to preserve our democratic way of life, fought to preserve the red ensign? How can our Prime Minister turn a deaf ear on their pleas to retain the flag which they fought for, when over 100,000 men and women made the supreme sacrifice? The majority of veterans in Canada and their families, who account for several million of our total population, will be very bitter toward any government that scraps the red ensign completely.
I would like to read a short letter published in the Peterborough Examiner, sent to me from an adjoining riding represented by the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Honey). He asked me to use this in my speech if I spoke in the house on the flag. I feel it is a little too strong so I shall only read part of it:
Our government will, beyond a shadow of doubt, break faith with all who sacrificed so much during the two world wars if it takes away our flag. The idea of parliament not allowing the Canadian people the right to choose their own flag is nothing but dictatorship-
If a new flag is chosen it will have to have a name. If the one with three maple leaves is chosen it will have to be called "The Triple D."
The first leaf will be called dictator because of the way the flag is being introduced.
The second leaf will be called division because it has already divided the nation.
The third leaf will be called destroyer because our freedom and rights will be destroyed.
I feel this design and the way it was brought out is creating a division in our country today, and I would like to say a word to the Prime Minister, that he is not being fair to our veterans. Who else in our dominion have more right to give their opinions about the flag than those people who fought our wars for us? This is another reason why we should have a plebiscite.
I am sorry the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) is not in the house this evening because I wish to mention some parts of her speech. She had this to say:
I think we, as members of parliament, should look at this whole question, regardless of our personal feelings in the matter, regardless even of what we think the majority of our constituents want.
She is taking the same attitude as our Prime Minister. It is quite evident that what

their constituents want is unimportant to them. The hon. lady also stated:
A referendum, Mr. Speaker, is only really suitable in a culturally and socially homogeneous society.
I consider this utter nonsense. A person is either in favour or not in favour of the flag, regardless of his cultural or social level. Every Canadian is worthy of a vote in this plebiscite.
I would like to refer the hon. lady to an article in the Peterborough Examiner headed, "Incensed Legion Writes Pearson About New Flag".
Cobourg Legion, branch 133 with 500 members, is "incensed" over the possible plight of Canada's war memorials with the advent of Prime Minister Lester Pearson's maple leaf flag.
A letter in the same newspaper states:
The Cobourg branch of the Royal Canadian Legion has written to the president of the dominion command asking that some thought be given to the matter of the position that the many war memorials throughout Canada would be placed in should this proposed flag be forced upon us, who do not feel the desire to have the change.
For our protection and for those who feel alike it is suggested that the dominion government enter into some guarantee to the general public that all memorials, wherever placed retain the same scheme of draping that they at present have.
That places designated as a gift of the government or as a war memorial-people that now fly the Canadian ensign or the union jack be so authorized to continue.
That the next of kin of those whose names feature upon roles of honour in churches, public halls and such places be asked their respective opinions on a majority basis before any change of drape is allowed.
This letter is written, at the wish of more than 500 members, who feel that they have given some of the years of their lifetime in the service of their country and who now continue in the service of the Royal Canadian Legion as true sons of Canada, sworn to obey the laws of our country and to protect the servicemen and their families to the best of their abilities.
Yours very truly,
J. M. Gaiger, Public Relations Officer, Branch 133, Cobourg, Ont.
I would like to ask the hon. member if she feels she has a better right to pick a flag for Canada than these veterans she represents in the house? With all due respect to the hon. lady the veterans and their families were not mentioned in her speech. They were bypassed completely and they are the people who should be making the decision-not a political party.
Scores of organizations in Canada representing millions of Canadians have passed resolutions and are sending them to the

government. They are requesting the retention of the red ensign as Canada's national flag. These signatures come from people in every province in Canada but they are being ignored by our Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). The right hon. gentleman stated that if the government were forced into an election he would make the flag an issue. I disagree with this. I believe our flag should never become a political football. I believe it should be kept free of politics. In my opinion, the free vote which was announced came too late because members of the Liberal party had been whipped into shape before the free vote was ever announced.
The Prime Minister realizes that every member has received letters and telegrams from Canadian Legion branches all across Canada. I know that these Legion branches and their members would be very fair with the government if they were approached in a proper manner and asked to sit down and help decide on a new emblem which would help bring about unity in our country. I also feel that every province would be fair about this if approached in the proper way. The English speaking people do not want a flag forced on them and I know that after listening to this debate the people of Quebec would not want to force an emblem on the people of this country which the majority of them cannot accept.
The members of the Canadian Legion are not the only ones whose opinions have been disregarded. I have here a letter which I think has been put on record several times before. It is from 12 people. One of them is Mr. D. G. Creighton, professor of history at the University of Toronto. Another, Mrs. Dyde, of Edmonton. Another signatory is Dr. Eugene Forsey, director of research, Canadian Labour Congress. Three of the signatories come from Peterborough, and this is why I am mentioning this letter. They are Mr. T. H. B. Symons, president of Trent University which will be opening in Peterborough this fall. Another is his assistant, Mr. Denis Smith. The third is a former member of this house, Mr. Walter Pitman, head of the history department of Kenner Collegiate. Mr. Pitman is a man very well regarded both in this house and in the city of Peterborough. This letter was sent to the Prime Minister on May 27. I will read two or three paragraphs from it. It begins:
We have thought deeply about the flag issue, and believe it necessary to write this open letter to you as an expression of our common feelings.
Canadian Flag
May we emphasize that we do not speak as political partisans, but only as concerned Canadians representing several parties.
Later on, the letter says:
We are not in the position of a country with a revolutionary tradition, creating itself anew; we exist because we have inherited the past without a revolutionary upheaval. It is false and dispiriting to adopt a flag which subtly ignores the truth of our own nature. This is not the kind of symbol to rally a bewildered and demoralized nation.
We respectfully suggest that you withdraw the maple leaf design for the time being, and that you convoke at once a private meeting of the parliamentary leaders of all parties to agree upon a new design which asserts our history. We profoundly believe that the present proposal will only deepen the spiritual malaise of Canada.
If the Prime Minister had sat down with these gentlemen or with the leaders of the parties to consider this question further we should not now be engaged in this long debate which is doing this country no good.
I have another letter here, this one from a young man. I do not believe the young people are supporting a new flag in the way the Liberal party would suggest. It says:
I am proud of your stand on the flag issue. I have never voted Conservative, but I assure you you will have my full support in any national referendum, or should Pearson shove it through parliament in the dictatorial manner which he proposes, I would stand behind you to the fullest.
I am in my early twenties. I speak for the young people of this community when I say: Keep the red ensign.
May I say that before this debate concludes I should like to hear more from supporters of the Liberal party. I should like to hear from cabinet ministers. I should like to hear from members representing Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. I should like to hear from more members from Ontario.
Do not forget British Columbia.

I should like to hear, also, from more members representing Quebec constituencies. My deskmate has spoken on the subject, and I have referred to that speech. As I say, I would appreciate hearing more speakers from Quebec. I cannot help but feel that their constituents are interested in a referendum or in having this issue sent to a parliamentary committee where there would be both representation from this house and from the Senate. In this way a national symbol could be chosen which would not be labelled a political pennant. It would be one fairly chosen by the people of this country, one which would link us together for the next hundred years, one we shall be proud of when we open our fair in the centennial year.

Canadian Flag
I feel that if this flag resolution is settled properly this country will remain united and become even stronger in the future.

On
June 17, 1964, I spoke on the resolution concerning a distinctive Canadian flag. At that time I gave many reasons why we should continue with the Canadian red ensign. As a 100 per cent Canadian of German descent 125 years ago, I felt that in accordance with our democratic way of life I should express my views according to the dictates of my conscience, regardless of political leanings, and other pressures so prominent during the debate of such an important question.
In talking over this question with many of my constituents during the odd week end, I found support for the new flag as well as for the Canadian red ensign, and for that reason I came to the conclusion that a plebiscite or referendum should be held during the next election so that each and every Canadian could express his own opinion. Such a vote in my estimation is just as important now as was the referendum on concription years ago. I am sure we all realize that when such a vote is taken we as sound and loyal Canadians will abide by such a decision and bring unity to our country, probably to an extent we have never seen before.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said in this house that every member should have the opportunity to express his views on this important question. Up to the present time most hon. members on the other side, many of them in the government, have not done so. Why? Because it is my sincere belief that the flag they have chosen fails to express anything significant. In other words it is not an emblem or representation of anything real. So far, when any one of our members rises to speak on this issue all we hear from across the floor are the familiar words "Carried" and "Question". By making such remarks hon. members opposite are going contrary to the wishes of their own leader, who said all members in the house should be heard. It is their obligation to rise and make themselves heard so that the people in their constituencies may know what their opinions are on this important question. Then if a referendum should be held we could be guided by their suggestions or expressions of opinion.
The vote of the people is by far the fairest way in which to settle this problem once

and for all. Millions of people in Canada believe this is the only way of seeing as far as possible that this is not made a partisan issue. It has been suggested in certain quarters that a free vote of members or senators should be allowed. But as I explained in my previous address to this house, there would be a natural tendency, human nature being what it is, for government supporters to vote for their government's own design, and it is far from certain that a vote in the house on any issue of this nature would really reflect the feelings of the people of Canada. No doubt the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) had the following words in mind when he brought in an amendment in favour of holding a plebiscite. The May issue of the Royal Canadian Legion journal had this to say:
In a free, democratic country, where public opinion is neither regimented nor suppressed, instances occur when the people are stirred to the innermost depths of heart and soul. Then it is that government by the people, for the people, is given true effect by a national vote on the issue at stake, and on that only.
I was impressed with the remarks made by my good friend the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More), as I was by many other speeches that have been delivered since this debate was brought forward. Like the hon. member for Regina City, I believe that his subamendment has a great deal of merit, because we need to have further clarification. Yes, Mr. Speaker, we need to know what the plebiscite would be on. Let us look over this subamendment and carefully scrutinize its important points:
1.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?
2.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritages of both founding races?
3.	Are you in favour of the three maple leaves design?
4.	Are you in favour of a one maple leaf design?
The hon. member for Regina City has given the voters a wide scope for their choice, and I believe it is the most democratic way of solving this problem. No matter how we look at this great flag issue, we are reminded of the Gardens of the Dead. The commonwealth war graves commission annual report, so well prepared by this wonderful group of men, deals in considerable detail with the commission's work in all parts of the world where members of the armed forces of the British commonwealth are buried. How many Canadians realize that no less than 1,106,380 men from commonwealth countries fell in the first great war and are buried in 15,386 different cemeteries. In world

75Co
war II, 580,058 men from commonwealth nations made the supreme sacrifice and are buried in 15,551 cemeteries which also contain, however, 7,220 1914-1918 war graves.
I mention this fact, Mr. Speaker, "Lest we forget", and second so that we do not forget the many Silver Cross women whose hearts are still bleeding for these men who have been gone now for almost 50 years. I mention the Gardens of the Dead for the simple reason that they refer to men who fell in the first great war and in the second great war from commonwealth countries, of which we are proud to be one. With this in mind I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I was terrifically impressed with the flags floating outside the west block, where the third commonwealth education conference is being held at the present time. The red ensign, representing Canada, stands out above and beyond all other flags, having beauty and distinction.
And you can't mistake it.

And, as one hon. member has said, you cannot mistake it for any other flag, even at two miles or four miles distance. May I ask all those who wish to tear down the red ensign to give serious consideration to the part it has played in the growth of this great nation of ours. At the turn of this century thousands of immigrants left their homes in Europe with the hope of making a new life in Canada, and after the first world war another great immigration wave gave our population another tremendous lift. Then once again after the second world upheaval, Canada again became a haven of refuge and a chance for a new life.
Hon. members, I say to you that the magnet, the beacon, the beckoning light that brought those people to our shores was the red ensign. Hopeless and discouraged by conditions in their own lands, these new Canadians recognized in the union jack, an integral part of our flag, a promise of justice, freedom and opportunity for all men. We must never in any way appear to repudiate the part that the Magna Carta and the British parliamentary system have played in our development as a nation. As I said in my previous speech, Mr. Speaker, when I was wounded in the first great war the greatest people in the world to me at that time were the English, the Scots and the Irish. I was taken to hospital, and after four years of war I was treated in just the same manner as any man who was wounded in the 1914-18 war. From the bottom of my heart I say that the English, the Irish and the Scots are amongst the greatest people in the world.
Canadian Flag
As I left the parliamentary restaurant tonight my eyes wandered over the framed portraits in the adjacent gallery. I looked at the portraits of Gladstone, Pitt, Churchill and all those other great British prime ministers. If we are determined to uproot all our traditions and symbols, we should consider turning the faces of these men to the wall. Mr. Speaker, it might be well to remember that of Canada's male population of 30 or more years of age there are 25.6 per cent, or 1,056,768 veterans, according to the 1961 census. If we included the dependants of these men it would make these figures look quite impressive. The total of veterans includes all males who reported service in world war I, world war II, and the Korean operation, whether or not their service was with the Canadian forces.
Lest we forget, these men represented every province in Canada from Quebec, the mari-times and all across this country to British Columbia. The unity and co-operation of these men brought success to the army, the air force and the navy. Mr. Speaker, I do not believe for a minute that all these fine men are in favour of the continuance of the Canadian red ensign; but I assure you that a great majority will show how they stand if a plebiscite is forthcoming. Let us not be deceived, as facts always tell the truth in regard to such an important question.
Remembrance day is just around the comer. It plays a big part in such an important issue, as we should remember in these few hours before the flag is settled once and for all. It would be well to reflect on what Frederick E. Elmslie says in his circular for poppy day and Remembrance day, namely that Canada was not built in a straightforward, cut and dried manner, but rather has suffered cuts and bruises in its growing up. We are not a new country without a flag. Many countries have taken centuries to accomplish what we have done in 97 years-* strangely enough, much of it under the red ensign-and during these years of growth, Canada has always tried to make the world- as her men are today, serving in many parts of the globe-a better place for all of us in which to live.
It seems to me that abolishing the Canadian red ensign is as if one were to propose a bill to abolish the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, because the musical ride originated from men riding as a pastime on Sunday afternoons. Yes, and how would the suggested new flag represent the thousands of people who reside in hundreds of square

Canadian Flag
miles in our country where there are no maple trees? Nearly all the speeches in this house have explained the red ensign and what it stands for. Why design a new flag when the ensign already has on it three leaves on a white background?
Mr. Speaker, it is rather hard to make a speech when there are so many others going on over there.

Surely not all suggestions which are made are improvements or represent progress.
What surely could be more uniting than the fact that working side by side to build this great country in one century have been Indians, French, English, Negroes, ethnics and Jews, people who fought, shed their blood and immortalized the bloody beaches, trenches and battlefields of the world so that we might have what we now possess? I could bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker-a fact which you already know-that at the battle of Ypres 50 years ago green Canadian troops attacked, and later many of them choked and died as a yellowish-green fog of poisonous chlorine filled the trenches. I can recall many battles waged under similar circumstances, all of which demonstrate the terrific sacrifices made by our brave men, our brothers and cousins and friends under the red ensign for their country and for upholding freedom of religion, freedom of speech and freedom of the press.
I can well remember, Mr. Speaker, serving in the front line trenches with Indians, French, Negroes, ethnics and Jews made up of Protestant, Catholic and Jewish faiths, and when any of these men were wounded no one questioned their religion or race. When someone was wounded all of his pals came to his assistance, showing the true value of fellowship, companionship and unity. These and others are the type of men who should have a real say about our future flag. A plebiscite would give them this right. Thousands of our comrades will never come back to tell us about the horrors of war, but we certainly know some of them paid the greatest price- death. Is this in itself not enough to make the ensign official? Or was this, the greatest of human sacrifices, meaningless and wasted?
The least we can do now is to show our humble gratitude, reverence and respect. I say in all sincerity: Let the ensign alone and make it official. If the ensign was not distinguished in the beginning before the wars, it certainly was distinguished after the wars.

Canada's sons have fought and died under the ensign for our freedom. Surely it is now unquestionably distinctive, and distinguished enough for us. Lest we forget, remember for a moment before a decision is made.

Mr. Speaker, I make no apologies for rising to take part in this debate because it is no ordinary debate. The subject under discussion at this time is the flag resolution, the amendment and the subamendment and is something which will not be dealt with by every parliament. When parliament passes a bill and the legislation concerned does not do the job it was designed to do, then the following session or the session after that parliament can bring in amendments to correct the deficiency. The flag is different. Once we adopt the flag, that flag will be here to stay for scores of years, even centuries. Therefore it is most important that this subject be thoroughly debated, and I would certainly like to see more members from the government benches rising to take part in this debate.
So far, Mr. Speaker, there have been many outstanding speeches, but I do not intend to start naming those who have made such excellent speeches. Incidentally, all of the good speeches have been coming from this side of the house because, as the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) said, on the other side there is a filibuster of silence.
I am in the same position as that of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), the hon. member for Marquette, the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) and many others. I do not belong to either one of the founding races, and I belong to a different nationality than they. Both my parents came from Iceland, a small island in the north Atlantic which is of great importance to the western world. Iceland is a country with the comparatively small population of 185,000 people. It is a country which cherishes freedom and democracy. Great Britain is referred to as the mother of parliaments. Iceland can truly be called the grandmother of parliament because Iceland established the first democratic parliament in the world in the year 930. The old Icelandic sages indicate that Leif Ericson came to North America in the year 1000, which is a long time before Columbus discovered America in 1492.
I have indicated that both my parents came from Iceland. My father came as a young boy in 1886 and my mother at the turn of the century. Both my wife's parents also came

from Iceland. They came to this country because they felt there would be greater opportunity here than in their own native land. I am sure that practically all those who came to this country are glad they came. They have made a living for themselves and have fitted into this country very well. Incidentally, the first Icelanders when they arrived in Canada settled in Ontario briefly, and then settled in Gimli, Manitoba, where they were given a tract of land which was designated as an Icelandic reserve. This was in October of 1875, and the Icelandic reserve started at Boundary Creek. They were given land along lake Winnipeg and some islands in lake Winnipeg; and they were actually a sovereign state. They remained a sovereign state and had their own self-government, establishing their own schools during those years. However they became very loyal to this country and have participated very actively in everything.
I was surprised the other day to hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) give the members of the House of Commons a lecture about the length of debate. In fact I got the impression that he thought debate should be limited, although he did specify that this specific debate now in progress should not be limited. In view of all the talking he does in this house I feel he is not on firm ground when lecturing the house about the length of the debate. I suggest to him that if there were 265 members like himself in this house, who love to talk, no session of parliament could be completed, and certainly would not be completed within the year. If members like that hon. member wish to contribute to the reformation of parliament they should commence by restraining themselves. People who love to talk generally do so for the sake of publicity.
Mr. Speaker, the only suggestion referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) referred to was that in respect of extending the sitting hours. The Minister of Justice made an amazing speech last Thursday during this debate. He suggested that his party would be willing to consider other legislation on Monday, provided the hours of sitting were extended on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays from eight until midnight. I should like to point out that during our consideration of the estimates of the Department of Industry on Friday afternoon, attendance in this house was very poor. At one time there were five members present in the government benches, and for a time there was not a single member
Canadian Flag
of the New Democratic party, of the Social Credit party or of the Creditiste party in this chamber. Before these members commence to suggest longer hours perhaps they should attempt to sit in this house and pay attention to what is taking place.
The amendment moved by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) is:
That all the words after "that" in line one be deleted and the following substituted:
"As the proposal to change Canada's national flag will affect the unity and destiny of Canada now and for years to come, the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to conduct a plebiscite prior to any further action being taken by the House of Commons, in order that all Canadians may be given their rightful opportunity to declare their choice concerning a national flag."
I certainly feel that every member of this house should be able to support that amendment.
The subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) proposed:
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the words:
"and that in such a plebiscite among the questions to be placed before the people should be the following:
1.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?
2.	Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign with changes made thereon to show the main heritages of both founding races?
3.	Are you in favour of the three maple leaves design?
4.	Are you in favour of a one maple leaf design?"
I was very pleased while listening to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) to hear him say he had been back to his riding and the people with whom he spoke urged him to support the suggestion that a plebiscite be held.
I was not away as long as that hon. member but I did spend a Saturday and Sunday in my riding. The people with whom I spoke certainly are in favour of a plebiscite. They feel we should move on to more important business and settle this flag issue by referendum at the time of the next general election. That would not be too costly and would certainly settle this question once and for all.
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested to hear the hon. member for Kootenay West relate his experience in respect of the three maple leaves design flags that have been flying here in the capital city, and I certainly agree with his theory that once the price of an article is cut, that is an indication the demand is decreasing. When the price of an article is cut down as low as 19 cents I would suggest that

Canadian Flag
is an indication there is practically no demand. Surely this is a clear indication to the Prime Minister and the treasury bench that they should act on this subamendment and refer this issue to the people.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that there are people in my riding of many racial origins and backgrounds. The 1961 census shows a total of 50,320 people in the federal constituency of Selkirk, broken down as follows: British Isles, 15,790; French, 3,747; German, 3,506; Italian, 57; Jewish, 122; Netherlands, 1,220; Polish, 3,304; Russian, 242, Scandinavian, 6,847; Ukrainian, 7,922; other European, 1,437; Asiatic, 118; native Indians, 5,765, and others and not stated, 243.
There are many religious denominations in my riding including Anglican Church of Canada, Baptist, Greek Orthodox, Jewish, Lutheran, Mennonite, Pentecostal, Presbyterian, Roman Catholic, Ukrainian (Greek) Catholic, United Church of Canada and others. These people with this variety of background and religion in this part of Canada live together, work together and play together in peace, understanding and harmony. They all think of themselves as Canadians first, and think in terms of one Canada. These people are tolerant and understanding. They are not rigid or inflexible. They believe in principles and they believe in God. They believe that symbols should be steeped in history and tradition. These people are all loyal to the flag of Canada.
The red ensign, as has been pointed out by many previous speakers, has been used by Canada since confederation, and was declared as Canada's official flag by order in council dated September, 1945. The thought of destroying or removing this flag arouses deep emotions in many people. This is the most controversial and emotional topic that has come before parliament since I came here in 1958. I fail to understand the Prime Minister in his determination to force this issue, despite the knowledge of the tremendous opposition to both the method by which this resolution was introduced and the design itself. For the Prime Minister to continue this stand is nothing but straight dictatorship. The opposition has moved an amendment proposing a national plebiscite, and a subamendment suggesting the form of that plebiscite. These suggestions have been made in an attempt to extricate the Prime Minister from the dilemma in which he finds himself.
I should also like to point out that I have received a great deal of mail in respect of this flag issue. I have received far more letters

on this subject than on any other, and all the letters with few exceptions have expressed favour for retention of the red ensign. I have received only one letter from my constituents favouring the three maple leaves design. All the others are for the red ensign and oppose the suggested flag. I believe every Canadian Legion branch in my riding has written supporting the red ensign and requesting that it be retained as the flag of Canada.
I do not intend to read the letters I have received except one short one from Home-brook in my constituency. It reads as follows:
I hear on this morning's radio that the flag issue is again to the fore. Am enclosing clipping which expresses my sentiments. I certainly will never fly Pearson's choice for a flag. Our family and neighbours always flew the red ensign and I would not object to some symbol being added recognizing French contribution to our country.
Shame on all those who would forsake the flag which represents all that has protected us for hundreds of years. How long will it be before they tire of this new flag?
In his letter he encloses a letter that appeared in the Western Producer of July 16, 1964. I think it is appropriate that I read that letter too because this gentleman said that it expressed his opinions. The letter to the Western Producer is headed "Flag Won't Promote Unity" and reads as follows:
Though I have never been a rabid sentimental flag waver I find I did not realize just how much the old flag meant to me until the almost certainty of losing it forever was brought home to me by recent events.
For more than 60 years I have observed it flying from many a flagpole all across the country. Always the sight of it brings to me the same feeling that comes to me when I see and hear a flight of Canada geese winging on their way-a mystic sense and realization of the immensity of our country and its past history. To me the old flag is more than an old bit of bunting. It stands for and exemplifies the hopes and aspirations of many generations of every ethnic group who have sought for and found security and happiness beneath its folds. Unfortunately it is an historial fact that to a large section of our population the old flag or even the red ensign is and always has been obnoxious for reasons that are quite obvious.
For this reason and the fact that our present federal government owes its very existence to these people we are to have a new flag of strange design thrust upon us, a design that features prominently three maple leaves. Most of us in western Canada have never seen a genuine maple leaf, yet this is supposed to convey a feeling of unity from sea to sea.
The government is evidently determined to pursue this matter to its ultimate end-a new flag. Quebec must be appeased no matter how many other feelings are hurt.

We cannot prevent the institution of a new flag -but no one can make us love or respect it. Nor will it promote unity. More likely the reverse.
George Watson.
I have many more letters I could read but I will go on with something else. As I said, I have received many letters from my constituency and all of them ask for the retention of the red ensign, except one in favour of the new three maple leaves flag.
Read it.

The odds are at least 100 to 1 so maybe you would like to read it. There are some questions I should like answered. Who asked the Prime Minister for a new flag? That question has been asked before but no answer has been forthcoming. I know that the Prime Minister visited Selkirk during the 1962 election campaign and again in the 1963 election campaign, and he certainly made no mention of a new flag during either one of those visits. He made one specific promise in Selkirk in 1963 which was reported by the Canadian Press. He promised to establish a committee of inquiry to investigate the effects of railway branch line abandonment, but to my knowledge such a committee was never established. However, 1 suppose in that regard we should accept the view of the Postmaster General (Mr. Nicholson) who said the other day that when you are in opposition and trying to get enough members to form the government you make promises to get votes, but after you assume office it is not necessary to fulfil those promises. The Prime Minister was in opposition at that time and I suppose he was only trying to get himself elected to office.
The Prime Minister has indicated that he promised a new flag within two years. I would suggest that the promise of a flag is in the very same category as the promises to which the Postmaster General referred the other day. There is another question I should like answered. Why did the flag issue become urgent all of a sudden and take priority over all other legislation? This question has also been asked before but certainly no answer has been forthcoming from the Prime Min-istre or anyone else on the government side.
Politics.
They have got no legislation ready.
Just a smokescreen.

Is it a coincidence that this piece of legislation became urgent shortly after the visit or safari of the Minister of
Canadian Flag
Forestry (Mr. Sauve) and the Prime Minister's chief adviser to Quebec city last April? According to Time magazine, when they made that visit to Quebec city they almost collided with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickers-gill), but he was shooed out another door because he is too clumsy and has not got the technique or the finesse to be able to negotiate with the premier of Quebec.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Brelon North and Victoria):
speechtext: Is that three flag Jack?
Did this visit have something to do with the flag question becoming urgent? If it did, the people of Canada certainly have a right to know and there should be an answer forthcoming.
There never will be. No answers; all promises.

Many editorials have appeared supporting the stand we have taken in asking for a referendum as set out in the subamendment and the amendment. However, I only want to read one short editorial because I do not want to take too much time in this regard. Many editorials have appeared in newspapers across Canada saying that the only logical answer, the only fair proposition, is to refer this matter to the people and let the people decide what type of flag they want. In today's Toronto Telegram there is an editorial headed "Stop It" which reads as follows:
The flag debate has gone on far, far too long. The Canadian people are wearied of it and people abroad must be looking at the performance of our 26th parliament with sniggering amazement.
Prime Minister Pearson's stubborn insistence that the Pearson pennant, or some modification of it must be approved before parliament rises is reckless and extravagant of time and money. The issue could be dealt with fairly if Mr. Pearson would agree to a plebiscite through which Canadians from coast to coast could express their preference for retention of the Canadian ensign or some new banner. The cost and inconvenience involved in such a poll would be less than that occasioned by wasted hours in fruitless debate and the stalling of parliament's business.
If Mr. Pearson is afraid of loss of face in taking this course, the matter could be put in the hands of an all-party committee. The recommendation of the committee then could be incorporated in a plebiscite.
It has been said that a plebiscite would be divisive. The late prime minister Mackenzie King did not hesitate to call a plebiscite on a far more explosive issue-military conscription-in the emotionally charged war years.
That article certainly suggests that the Prime Minister should accept the subamendment and the amendment, and that he

Canadian Flag
should refer this matter to the people themselves. It also refers to a committee. These suggestions have been made in the house.
Seven more minutes.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, you saw fit to call attention to the remarks being made on this side of the house in support of the speaker. For the last five minutes the speaker has had trouble getting himself across-
How do you know?

-because of the continuous interjections like the one we have just heard. I think it is about time members on this side enjoyed the same privilege as members on that side, and that they be called to order when it is absolutely necessary that they should be.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to point out to the hon. member that when the Chair called for order it was calling on members from the other side of the house.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, now that the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) is back from his extended holiday, I would point out that his remarks have been preventing me from hearing the interesting speech to which we have been listening.

That certainly was no point of order.
People in public life generally have the same aims and objectives. They may approach these in a different manner, but one of the objectives of those in public service is to improve the lot of their fellow man. This flag controversy is making many people unhappy and is creating bitterness and hatred. Surely these are not the aims and objectives of any public servant.
In view of this I would strongly urge the Prime Minister to withdraw the resolution at this time. He would be doing his country a great service if he would do this. Many millions of Canadians are unhappy with the method the Prime Minister has used in introducing this resolution, and many millions are also unhappy with the proposed design. They feel that it is a sickly and insipid looking flag.
Some say the design is not important, but I say those people are wrong. The design should have a meaning, should be distinctive in appearance, and should be something which the majority of Canadians want and will

respect. When a new flag is chosen by parliament it will fly from flagpoles in this country for many years, perhaps even for centuries to come. This resolution is not like other pieces of legislation. When parliament passes an act, and then a few months later it is found not to be doing exactly what it was intended to do, an amendment can be brought in to correct it. Not so with a flag. Therefore extreme care should be used in the selection and adoption of a new flag.
A flag should not be associated with any political party, and the design should not be associated with any one individual. The hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) has clearly indicated that the selection of the proposed design was not submitted to the Liberal caucus before being introduced in the House of Commons. It has been pointed out that the design is the personal choice of the Prime Minister. Seeing that it is his personal choice, it then becomes labelled with the government of which he is the head, and also with the Liberal party. It has therefore become a political flag.
Many thousands of Canadians have written to their members of parliament urging them to do everything in their power to prevent the adoption of the proposed three maple leaf flag. I firmly believe that these people are right, that the adoption of this proposed three maple leaf flag would be a calamity. It can .only bring about division, disunity and dissension. I feel that it is my duty, and the duty of every member of parliament, to adopt a course to prevent this from happening.
When the time comes when the majority of Canadians want a new flag, let us act in a mature manner and select one flag, without any thought of appeasement to any region or section of the country. The manner in which the resolution was introduced clearly indicates the lack of understanding of the situation by the government, and also its indecisiveness.
It has been suggested that the matter of a flag became urgent through the pressure of the premier of Quebec. It has also been suggested that the inclusion of the second flag in the resolution was at the request of the premier of Newfoundland. Be that as it may, the timing of the introduction of this resolution could not have been worse.
The appointment of the royal commission on biculturalism and bilingualism was completely wrong. The expenditure of the taxpayers' money on this type of commission is unjustified. With a population such as we have in Canada, with so many racial origins, there is no room for this type of commission.

Since it was appointed it has certainly stirred up the pot. Also, with the extremists and separatists movement having been active in Quebec during the past few months and receiving nation-wide publicity, the introduction of a flag resolution was looked upon by many millions of Canadians with suspicion and disfavour. Under this type of climate it is impossible to get any resemblance of unity, support or respect for the resolution introduced by the Prime Minister.
Before the Prime Minister introduced the resolution he said there would be a free vote on this subject. Later he reversed that decision and said his government would stand or fall on this resolution and, if the resolution were defeated, he would take it as a vote of nonconfidence and call an election. A few days ago he again reversed his decision and now says there will be a free vote. But it was ably pointed out by the Liberal member for York-Humber that there could not be a free vote on this resolution, that the resolution stood in the name of the Prime Minister and was seconded by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau). It therefore was a government motion and no free vote could be held.
If there is a general desire on the part of the Prime Minister for a free vote, he should withdraw the resolution and have it resubmitted by a backbencher. Many members have made suggestions and recommendations to help the Prime Minister and the government get out of the impasse in which
Canadian Flag
they find themselves. The amendment moved by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) to hold a referendum or plebiscite, was moved for this purpose. Having been denied the right of a free vote in parliament, and the proposed flag having become a political flag, and with the impasse the government find themselves in, the only proper and honourable course to follow is to refer this to the people themselves and let them make the choice. The subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) spells out more clearly how the ballot could be taken, and I have many editorials here supporting the stand that a plebiscite should be held.
I would strongly urge members from all parties to support the subamendment. This would put into operation the most democratic principle of all, where the decision on a flag rests with the people themselves. This could be done most easily and economically at the time of the next general election. Once the vote was over, I feel certain that practically every Canadian would be willing to accept the rule of the majority, which would leave this country united and strong.
